rows.implication: Even on the corrected, higher cash figure the yield is 2.4-2.5% against a 4.93% risk-free rate; the valuation conclusion is unchanged, the earnings-quality claim is stronger by about $13bn.
rows.confidence: high - both figures read from the 10-Q and reconciled to the FY2025 10-K
rows.follow_up: Does the FY2026 10-K identify the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities as deferred consideration, and when is it payable?

rows.finding: The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn while IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it against 10% a year earlier.
rows.mechanism: Growth is price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while the hardware cost base rises; price-led growth is the most reversible kind and compresses margin as memory costs bite.
rows.benchmark: IDC unit market -16.7%; TrendForce component costs; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter.
rows.weakens: Services at 40.3% of the gross-profit pool offsets hardware margin pressure, and the September quarter is guided to 9-11% growth.
rows.implication: FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is the risk to the 33% margin input in the DCF; a 200bp miss is $0.52 of EPS.
rows.confidence: medium - third-party forecasts and a component-cost model, not company disclosure
rows.follow_up: How much of FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices, and what gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter?

rows.finding: Apple's own four-year mean P/E is 31.0x, which on implied FY2027 EPS of $9.79 is $303 a share, 12% below the 2026-10-30 price; FY2022 ended at 24.6x and FY2023 at 27.9x.
rows.mechanism: Multiple reversion, not earnings, is the swing factor: a return to 31.0x costs 12% and to 24.6x costs 30%, swallowing years of shareholder yield.
rows.benchmark: Apple's fiscal year-end multiples FY2022-FY2025 (24.6x, 27.9x, 37.5x, 34.2x) and the current 39.5x.
rows.weakens: The mean is computed over only four years, all of them in a rising multiple regime.
rows.implication: The realistic bear case is a 30% drawdown to about $242, which sets position sizing and the sell discipline.
rows.confidence: high - computed from filed year-end prices and EPS

plan.comparison_set: Peers Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon, Dell and HP; Apple's own five fiscal-year multiples and four-year mean; DCF at 7.0-9.5% discount rates and 3-5% terminal growth.
plan.counter_evidence: Quality franchises have held 30x-plus multiples through a high-rate regime, the cost of equity is a judgement rather than an observation, and the buyback plus a persistent working-capital source add real cash return.
plan.visual: Valuation methods table plus the WACC and terminal-growth sensitivity grid.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned; drafting or revision references; any figure without a source; the withdrawn $111.5bn normalisation.

rows.finding: Apple's iPhone 18 cycle launched on 2026-09-09 at higher prices: iPhone 18 Pro from $1,199 and Pro Max from $1,299, plus the first foldable, iPhone Duo; the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second Air slipped to spring 2027. iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the June 2026 quarter, +22% year on year, and $196.5bn for nine months, +22%.
rows.mechanism: Apple is defending revenue with price and form-factor mix (Pro, Pro Max, foldable) rather than unit growth, and spreading launches across two events to keep ASP and supply of 2nm parts under control.
rows.benchmark: Prior iPhone 17 cycle and FY2025 iPhone growth; Q3 FY2026 iPhone +22% versus total company +16.4%.
rows.weakens: MacRumors reports Apple raised prices and repriced the iPhone 17 to $899 while memory costs rise, so unit elasticity is untested; the Duo's durability and yield are unproven.
rows.implication: The hardware cycle is not maturing yet; it is being re-priced. Watch Q4 FY2026 (2026-11-02) for whether mix held through launch.
rows.confidence: high — launch and pricing from Apple's own release; revenue from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What are Duo first-quarter units and return/warranty rates, and did Pro mix hold in the December 2026 quarter?

rows.finding: The rebuilt Siri shipped on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English only, running on a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed 2026-01-12; Bloomberg reported the model at 1.2 trillion parameters and about $1bn a year (neither company confirmed the price). Apple's own foundation-model papers describe on-device and server models.
rows.mechanism: Apple keeps the interface, personal context and Private Cloud Compute wrapper, but licenses frontier reasoning from a competitor; the differentiation moves from model quality to distribution and privacy architecture.
rows.benchmark: Google owns the model, the TPUs and Android; Apple owns the device and the assistant surface but rents the intelligence.
rows.weakens: A 1.2-trillion-parameter rented model versus a published on-device model shows the hardest queries are outsourced; the beta label two years after Apple Intelligence launched is a delay, not a launch.
rows.implication: Siri is a feature that protects the installed base, not a moat that expands it. Price Apple as a hardware-and-services company with an AI option.
rows.confidence: high on dates and the deal; medium on the $1bn and parameter count (press reports, not company disclosure)
rows.follow_up: When does Siri AI leave beta, what proportion of queries route to Gemini, and what does Apple disclose about the cost?

rows.finding: Apple spent $34.04bn on R&D in the first nine months of FY2026, +33% year on year, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Its foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud.
rows.mechanism: Apple is running an opex-heavy AI strategy: pay for models and rented compute rather than build datacentres, which protects free cash flow but caps frontier scale and hands bargaining power to Google.
rows.benchmark: Hyperscalers capitalise AI infrastructure; Apple's nine-month capex is about 2% of revenue while R&D is running at roughly 30% growth.
rows.weakens: The R&D step-up is a real cost: +$8.4bn in nine months, with no separately disclosed AI revenue to offset it, so margin is the place the bill lands.
rows.implication: Free cash flow stays intact and buybacks continue, but there is no proprietary compute moat to underwrite a higher multiple on AI.
rows.confidence: high — both figures are in the 10-Q cash-flow and income statements
rows.follow_up: What share of the R&D increase is AI infrastructure and depreciation, and does Apple intend to keep renting frontier models after the Gemini term?

rows.finding: Silicon stays the deepest in-house layer: A20 Pro in the iPhone 18 Pro on a 2nm process versus A19 on 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line. Products gross margin rose on mix and tariff refunds, partly offset by memory costs.
rows.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon converts into either margin or performance at fixed price; the modem insourcing removes a Qualcomm royalty and gives Apple control over cellular power and cost.
rows.benchmark: A19 (3nm) to A20 (2nm) is a full node step; the modem shift ends Apple's dependence on an external cellular supplier.
rows.weakens: Component costs are rising: the 10-Q warns of advanced-semiconductor, NAND and DRAM constraints expected to intensify. A node advantage does not protect gross margin when memory prices spike.
rows.implication: Silicon is the moat that is still widening; it supports the products margin line rather than revenue growth.
rows.confidence: medium — 2nm and C2 are press-reported; margins are from the 10-Q
rows.follow_up: What is the C2 versus Qualcomm cost delta per unit, and how much of the FY2027 products margin assumption depends on tariff refunds that may not repeat?

rows.finding: U.S. patent grants fell to 2,722 in 2025 from 3,082 in 2024 (-12%), placing Apple seventh; the foldable Duo's hinge is made with AI-matched parts, confocal laser scanning and 3D-printed photopolymer micro-layers rather than protected by a single blocking patent.
rows.mechanism: The durable IP sits in process know-how and integration, which is harder to design around but also harder to assert; the portfolio is broad rather than deep in any one blocking area.
rows.benchmark: Apple's grant count is declining while U.S. patent activity overall declined; Huawei and TSMC rank ahead of Apple in the same 2025 table.
rows.weakens: A falling grant count is not proof of a weakening moat, but it removes the patent-count argument for one; the hinge know-how must be proven in field reliability.
rows.implication: Underwrite the moat on switching costs and manufacturing yield, not on patent breadth.
rows.confidence: medium — aggregate counts are third-party (IFI) data; individual patent families were not retrieved
rows.follow_up: What is the granted-versus-pending mix in the foldable and on-device-AI families, and are there blocking third-party hinge or display patents?

rows.finding: Health features are shipping and regulated: Apple Watch hypertension notifications were FDA-cleared, with peer-reviewed commentary in Hypertension treating the clearance as a juncture for cuffless screening and questioning accuracy and utility; the feature notifies over a 30-day signal rather than measuring blood pressure.
rows.mechanism: Health adds a regulated, trust-based reason to upgrade a watch every few years and raises the cost of leaving the ecosystem, but it is sold inside a hardware product rather than as a therapy.
rows.benchmark: Apple Watch is described as the most widely adopted consumer health device; the clinical evidence level is a cleared screening notification, not a diagnostic claim.
rows.weakens: Contested clinical value limits pricing power and invites litigation and regulator scrutiny; it is a differentiator, not a new revenue pool.
rows.implication: Wearables and health support the installed base and ASP without changing the growth slope on their own.
rows.confidence: medium — clearance reported by a peer-reviewed journal; the FDA record itself returned no match in the openFDA device search
rows.follow_up: What is the attach and upgrade rate for watches with the hypertension feature, and what does the FDA clearance letter allow Apple to claim?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's silicon/OS/AI stack a durable moat, or is Apple falling behind in AI while the hardware cycle matures?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer that the next upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it.
plan.why_different: This section judges mechanism and replicability of the technology itself — how the silicon, OS and AI layers work and what can be copied — not market size, valuation or the industry's growth rate.
plan.mechanism: Vertical integration in silicon and OS converts into margin or performance at a fixed price and into switching costs; buying frontier models and renting TPU compute converts a would-be fixed-cost AI moat into a variable cost paid to a competitor, which protects cash flow but leaves the differentiation in hardware, privacy and distribution.
plan.comparison_set: Google (owns Gemini, TPUs and Android), Samsung (licenses Google's stack), Huawei (constrained by domestic process), Microsoft (cloud capex model), and Apple's own prior cycle (iPhone 17, A19 3nm, no foldable).
plan.counter_evidence: AI talent left for Meta through 2025; the Siri rebuild shipped as an English beta in September 2026, two years after Apple Intelligence launched; capex fell while R&D rose; patent grants fell 12%; the Duo's hinge durability is unproven; memory costs threaten products margin.
plan.visual: Performance-metrics table plus the moat table with the replication test (funded team of 50), and the evidence component on the Google dependency.
plan.prohibited: AI leader, seamless ecosystem, strong team, huge market, well positioned, innovative company, best-in-class without a metric, 'many patents', 'about' before a figure, any sentence describing how the section is written.

rows.finding: Average daily volume 40.41m shares ($13.84bn) over 20 days and 41.34m shares ($13.56bn) over three months; price sits 3.5% above the 50-day average of $333.04 and 16.2% above the 200-day of $296.56.
rows.mechanism: A $5tn mega-cap with 40m shares a day traded has an exit that is always open at the screen price; the cost of exit is the spread and any de-rating, not the ability to sell.
rows.benchmark: A $250m position is 0.62% of the 20-day average value traded; a $1bn position is 2.5%.
rows.weakens: Liquidity evaporates in a correlated drawdown - in a market-wide selloff the bid thins and the discount to the last price widens, so ADV overstates achievable exit size in stress.
rows.implication: Liquidity is not a constraint at any plausible position size: the fund can enter and exit in days with negligible market impact, so the exit risk is entirely a price risk, not a liquidity risk.
rows.confidence: high - timestamped market data
rows.follow_up: What position size is the fund contemplating, and does it breach any single-issuer or index-weight limit?

rows.finding: No holder owns control: 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding at 2026-01-02, Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10%, the largest holders being index managers; directors and officers hold about 0.06% between them.
rows.mechanism: With no controlling shareholder and a dispersed index base, price is set by flows and by the marginal institutional view of the multiple, not by a strategic buyer or a control contest.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 12-month low of $243.42 is 29.4% below the current price; the five-year closing low is $125.02.
rows.weakens: Index concentration cuts both ways: forced selling by passive funds in a redemption wave would hit Apple harder than a smaller, less-owned name.
rows.implication: Free float is effectively 100% and the marginal holder is an index or active fund, so the stock's buyer on exit is the same pool the fund sells into - index inclusion has been a structural bid, but it does not raise the price at which the business is worth owning.
rows.confidence: medium - the 52-week low overstates the chance of a full retracement but is the best local base rate
rows.follow_up: What is Apple's current S&P 500 weight, and what happens to passive demand if it is trimmed at a rebalance?

rows.finding: Total shareholder yield 1.9% (dividend 0.3% plus gross buyback 1.6%); net of $13.7bn of stock compensation the buyback yield is 1.36%; EPS grew 9.2% a year from FY2021 to the TTM, of which about 2.8 points a year came from the 12.8% reduction in diluted shares.
rows.mechanism: A long-only fund's return is dividend plus net buyback plus EPS growth plus the change in multiple; Apple supplies only 1.7 points of the first two, so nearly all of the return has to come from earnings growth or from a multiple that does not fall.
rows.benchmark: Trailing EPS CAGR over the five years to FY2021-TTM is 9.2% (S6, S1) versus revenue CAGR of 5.0% and net income CAGR of 6.4%.
rows.weakens: If the multiple expands further, the decomposition understates the return; 2026's 16.4% revenue growth suggests forward EPS growth may exceed 9%.
rows.implication: With a flat multiple the total return is about 10.7% a year (0.3% dividend, 1.4% net buyback, 9% EPS growth) - adequate; the whole question is whether 39.5x is a multiple that holds.
rows.confidence: high for the historic decomposition; medium for the forward multiple assumption
rows.follow_up: What EPS growth does consensus assume for FY2027 and FY2028, and does it require the buyback to keep running above $80bn?

rows.finding: A reversion from 39.5x to 31.0x costs 21.5% of price, about -7.7% a year over three years, which more than offsets the 1.7% shareholder yield and most of a 9% EPS growth rate.
rows.mechanism: Multiple compression is the mechanism by which a higher-rate regime reaches a long-duration equity: with the ten-year at 4.93% (+84bp y/y), the discount rate on Apple's terminal cash flows is higher than when the stock traded at 27.9x in FY2023.
rows.benchmark: Apple's fiscal year-end P/E: 24.6x (FY2022), 27.9x (FY2023), 37.5x (FY2024), 34.2x (FY2025); four-year mean 31.0x; AAPL currently 39.5x, a 27% premium to that mean.
rows.weakens: The stock has been 'expensive' versus its own history since FY2024 and has still returned 27.5% over the last twelve months; a mean-reversion model has been wrong for two years.
rows.implication: The asymmetry is the argument for selling into strength: at a five-year-high multiple the upside needs further expansion, while the downside is a reversion that is already observed once within the past four years.
rows.confidence: medium - multiples are certain, their persistence is not
rows.follow_up: What would keep the multiple above 35x for three years - sustained 10%-plus revenue growth, or a fall in the ten-year yield?

rows.finding: No plausible acquirer exists: every company in the peer set is smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market cap, so a takeover would require a buyer larger than any in the sector, plus antitrust clearance in the US, EU, China and UK.
rows.mechanism: The bid side of a $5tn equity is other portfolio managers, not strategics; index funds and buybacks are price-insensitive in direction but not in price, so the exit price is set by the same valuation debate the fund is making.
rows.benchmark: Largest technology peer Microsoft at $3,875.8bn market cap and $3,846.8bn EV; Alphabet $3,461.1bn; Meta $1,582.4bn.
rows.weakens: A sovereign wealth fund or a consortium could in principle bid, but at 39.5x earnings and a $5tn equity cheque the financing does not exist at a premium.
rows.implication: A control premium is not part of the return: the exit is at the market price, which means the fund's realisation depends entirely on the multiple other investors will pay.
rows.confidence: high - the comparison is arithmetic
rows.follow_up: Is there any activist or break-up case that would separate services from hardware, and who would fund a $5tn position?

rows.finding: Apple repurchased $82.2bn of stock in the TTM to 2026-06-27 against $15.6bn of dividends and $111.5bn of working-capital-normalised FCF, so the repurchase is at the limit of internally generated cash.
rows.mechanism: A fixed-dollar repurchase retires more shares as the price falls, so the EPS accretion per dollar rises and the floor under the per-share value is firmer than for a company that does not buy back.
rows.benchmark: $85bn a year is 1.7% of the $5.03tn capitalisation at $344.63, 3.0% at $270 and 3.6% at $240.
rows.weakens: The buyback is discretionary and could be cut in a downturn or redirected to AI capital spending; it also supports EPS, not the multiple, so it cannot prevent a de-rating.
rows.implication: The buyback is a standing, price-sensitive buyer that makes a de-rating self-limiting: each 10% fall in the price adds roughly 0.17 points to the buyback yield, which is why a bear case to $190-240 is more likely to be a long opportunity than a permanent loss.
rows.confidence: high for the arithmetic; medium for the $85bn run-rate
rows.follow_up: Will the May 2027 authorisation exceed the May 2025 $100bn programme, and will Apple fund it from cash or from debt?

rows.finding: On FY2029E EPS of $11.45 (my estimate: FY2026E $9.09 grown 9%/8%/7%), a 27x exit gives $309, a 31x exit $355 and a 34x exit $389; with about $3.50 of dividends over three years the three-year IRR from $344.63 is -3.2%, +1.3% and +4.5%.
rows.mechanism: Buying at a high multiple transfers the future return to the seller: the entry price fixes the IRR once the exit multiple and the earnings path are set, and at 39.5x the arithmetic leaves nothing for the buyer.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own FY2022-FY2025 P/E range of 24.6x-37.5x.
rows.weakens: If EPS grows faster than 9% - the June 2026 quarter grew EPS 28.7% - the IRR rises by roughly the excess growth rate for each year held.
rows.implication: From today's price the three-year return fails the 9% hurdle under every exit multiple below 39.5x; at a $270 entry the same range becomes +5.0% to +13.4% with a 10% central case.
rows.confidence: medium - exit multiples are a scenario assumption
rows.follow_up: What entry price does the fund's own hurdle rate require, and is a three-year or five-year holding period assumed?

rows.finding: No insider purchased a share in the six months to 2026-10-29; 37 sales totalled 590,642 shares and $183.45m, of which 34 transactions ($96.70m) were under Rule 10b5-1 plans; director Arthur Levinson sold $86.74m and Executive Chair Tim Cook $63.85m.
rows.mechanism: Insider behaviour is informative mainly at the extremes - a cluster of discretionary buys after a fall, or discretionary sales near highs; here the mix is plan-driven and uninformative about the multiple.
rows.benchmark: Peer insiders and the absence of open-market purchases across the six-month window.
rows.weakens: Almost all sales were scheduled 10b5-1 sales, and executives of a $5tn company sell for diversification regardless of valuation, so the signal is weak.
rows.implication: Management is not adding at $344; that is weak evidence against a near-term re-rating and consistent with a stock trading above what insiders consider value, though it is not a sell signal on its own.
rows.confidence: medium - plan sales are scheduled in advance and carry little information, discretionary sales carry more
rows.follow_up: Did any of the discretionary sales follow a change in the trading plan, and what is the executives' remaining unvested exposure?

plan.decision_question: For a long-only fund, what is the exit and total-return path, and what would force a sale?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer: with no company large enough to acquire it, the three-year return from $344.63 is -3% to +5% a year if the 39.5x multiple reverts toward its 31.0x four-year average, which sets the sell discipline at a price where the arithmetic clears 9% - roughly $270.
plan.why_different: Every other section asks whether Apple's business improves; this one asks how the fund gets its money back and at what price the risk/reward stops paying, and it must name the buyer or venue rather than list generic options.
plan.mechanism: There is no strategic exit for a $5tn company, so the only realisation routes are the market, Apple's own repurchase and the dividend. Return = dividend (0.31%) + net buyback (1.36%) + EPS growth, minus the annualised cost of any multiple compression; at 39.5x versus a 31.0x four-year mean, compression of about 7-8% a year can cancel the operating return.
plan.comparison_set: The last twelve months' own trading (52-week low $243.42, i.e. 29.4% below the current price), the FY2022-FY2025 multiple range (24.6x-37.5x, mean 31.0x), HP and Dell for hardware, Microsoft and Alphabet for the platform bid, and the 4.93% ten-year Treasury as the opportunity cost of holding a 1.9% shareholder yield.
plan.counter_evidence: A flat 39.5x multiple with 9-10% EPS growth still delivers about 10.7% a year, so the return is adequate while the multiple holds; the buyback is a self-correcting bid that accelerates as the price falls; and the June 2026 quarter's 16.4% revenue growth could keep the multiple elevated for longer than a mean-reversion model assumes.
plan.visual: Exit routes table (route, named buyer or venue, rationale, timing, likelihood, source) plus a return-sensitivity table by entry price and exit multiple.
plan.prohibited: No 'IPO or M&A', no unnamed acquirers, no invented index weight, no claim that a takeover premium is a return source, no repetition of the risk section's regulatory detail, no 'well positioned'.

rows.finding: In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple repurchased $62.1bn of stock, paid $0.27 a quarter in dividends, spent $34.04bn on R&D (+33%) and only $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn). In FY2025 it bought back $89.3bn under a $100bn authorisation and raised the dividend to $0.26.
rows.mechanism: Capital allocation reveals the bet: Apple funds AI from the income statement and returns the balance-sheet capacity to shareholders, treating frontier models as a purchased input rather than an owned platform.
rows.benchmark: FY2025: $89.3bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends against $34.55bn of R&D.
rows.weakens: A 33% R&D increase with falling capex means the marginal AI dollar is opex; if AI features do not lift hardware ASP, that spending is a pure margin drag.
rows.implication: The strategy is shareholder-return first, AI as an operating expense. It supports EPS and limits downside, but it does not build an asset that a competitor cannot rent too.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: Will Apple disclose AI-related depreciation or licensing cost separately, and does the buyback pace hold if margin compresses?

rows.finding: Apple assembled about 55m iPhones in India in 2025, up 53% and roughly a quarter of global output, using Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron; Indian assembly and components still cost more than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expire on 2026-03-31.
rows.mechanism: Geographic diversification reduces tariff and concentration risk but trades a mature supply chain for a subsidised, higher-cost one; the strategy is insurance bought with gross margin.
rows.benchmark: India assembled 36m iPhones in 2024; global iPhone output is 220-230m a year; all iPhone 17 models are now built in India.
rows.weakens: The shift is subsidy-dependent and costlier, so it does not improve unit economics; it also invites retaliation risk on the China side that the source does not quantify.
rows.implication: The tariff hedge is working on volume but is not yet a margin tailwind, and it depends on policy that expires within the next twelve months.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Has the subsidy regime been renewed, and what is the landed-cost gap between Indian and Chinese assembly for U.S.-bound units?

rows.finding: Services reached $91.73bn in nine months of FY2026 (+14%) at a 76.3% gross margin, with advertising and cloud services cited as the growth drivers; the EU DMA generated 56 interoperability requests by 2026-03-22, of which 43 were closed and 27 confidentially.
rows.mechanism: Services monetise the installed base at high incremental margin, but the DMA forces Apple to open interfaces and choice screens, which erodes the control that makes those services default.
rows.benchmark: iPhone revenue grew 22% in the same quarter; services gross margin is roughly 1.5 times the company average.
rows.weakens: Growth is concentrated in advertising and cloud, the areas most exposed to platform regulation and to the Google search distribution deal.
rows.implication: Services is the profit engine and the part regulation can tax; the DMA is a recurring engineering and legal cost, not a one-off.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: What is the revenue at risk from DMA-driven sideloading and default-choice changes, and how much of advertising growth is search-revenue-share dependent?

rows.finding: Apple confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to use Google Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year, while its own foundation models are trained on rented Google TPUs and its capex fell year on year.
rows.mechanism: Build-vs-buy resolved in favour of buy for the model and rent for the compute: Apple keeps capital light and ships sooner, at the cost of dependency on the company that also owns Android.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own July 2024 paper disclosing 8,192 TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips, rented through Google Cloud.
rows.weakens: Neither company confirmed the price or exclusivity, and the arrangement could be a bridge while Apple's own models improve — the 2026 Stepped MoE paper shows the research org still shipping efficiency work.
rows.implication: Partnering preserves cash and speed but cedes the frontier layer; the platform control that remains is the interface, the data boundary and the device.
rows.confidence: medium
rows.follow_up: Is the Gemini deal exclusive, what are its term and renewal date, and can Apple switch models without degrading Siri?

rows.finding: On 2026-01-14 the Commerce Department published initial Section 232 semiconductor findings that imposed no additional tariffs on Apple products; after the Supreme Court struck down certain IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, Apple applied for refunds and recognised them as a reduction of products cost of sales, while warning that memory and advanced-semiconductor supply constraints are expected to intensify.
rows.mechanism: Trade policy is being absorbed through the P&L rather than through supply-chain redesign alone; refunds flatter margin while the underlying cost of components rises.
rows.benchmark: The Section 232 investigation opened in 2025; the Supreme Court ruling of 2026-02-20 struck down certain IEEPA tariffs.
rows.weakens: The refund is non-recurring and the 10-Q flags further Section 232, Section 301 or sector tariffs as possible, so the relief may reverse.
rows.implication: Tariff policy is now a swing factor in reported gross margin, which makes one quarter's margin a poor guide to the next.
rows.confidence: high
rows.follow_up: How much of the products gross-margin improvement came from one-off tariff refunds, and what Section 301 measures now apply?

rows.finding: Apple reports fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results on 2026-11-02 having guided to 9-11% revenue growth, with iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and Duo on sale from 2026-09-18 and the standard iPhone 18 deferred to spring 2027.
rows.mechanism: Splitting the launch moves revenue between quarters and lets Apple sell higher-priced Pro and foldable models into the holiday window while 2nm supply matures for the cheaper models in spring.
rows.benchmark: FY2025 fourth-quarter revenue was $102.5bn, up 8% year on year.
rows.weakens: Guidance of 9-11% is below the 16.4% growth of the June 2026 quarter, which implies deceleration into the launch quarter rather than acceleration.
rows.implication: The next twelve months are checkable quarter by quarter; the launch split means the March 2027 quarter carries a second iPhone cycle that the prior year did not have.
rows.confidence: high

plan.decision_question: Does Apple's strategy convert AI and services into growth without ceding platform control?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model.
plan.why_different: This section judges execution and allocation — dated milestones, partners and what must be true in twelve months — rather than the technology's mechanism or the market's size.
plan.mechanism: Apple funds the AI layer from the income statement (R&D and licensing) rather than the balance sheet (datacentres), keeps control of the interface, distribution and privacy layer, and returns the resulting cash through buybacks; platform control is preserved while the frontier-model layer is ceded.
plan.comparison_set: Microsoft and Alphabet (capitalise AI infrastructure), Samsung (follows Apple's price and form factor), Huawei (rebuilds a domestic stack), and Apple's own prior capital-return cycle (FY2025 buybacks $89.3bn).

rows.finding: One class of common stock only: 50,400,000,000 shares authorised at $0.00001 par, 14,773,260,000 issued and outstanding at 2025-09-27 and 14,697,926,000 outstanding at 2026-01-02; Vanguard 9.63% and BlackRock 7.10% are the only disclosed 5% holders; all 12 directors and executive officers together hold 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% of the count.
rows.mechanism: One-share-one-vote with a diffuse register means no founder, family or supervoting class can block a bid, dictate capital allocation or install directors; control is exercised through the proxy and the indexed holders, so governance risk shows up as slow board refresh rather than as expropriation.
rows.benchmark: Alphabet, the closest mega-cap peer, still issues Class C stock alongside voting classes (2026 proxy), so a founder-controlled competitor can ignore short-term owners in a way Apple's holders cannot be forced to accept.
rows.weakens: BlackRock's 7.10% is computed from a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the holder table is partly stale and the true 2026 holder mix is not disclosed.
rows.implication: Clean title and an unblocked exit path support a multi-year holding; the price of that cleanliness is that no insider owns enough to align the board against management's preferences.
rows.confidence: high - figures read from the 10-K balance sheet and the 2026 proxy ownership table.
rows.follow_up: Has BlackRock's stake moved since 2023, and does any activist have a position below 5%?

rows.finding: Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus CEO Cook; independent tenure averages 12.0 years (Levinson since 2000, i.e. 26 years; Jung 2008; Sugar 2010; Wagner 2014), and two of the seven independents (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75.
rows.mechanism: A low-turnover board chaired by a 26-year director, with an executive chair who is the outgoing CEO after 2026-09-01, lowers the probability of external pressure on capital allocation, M&A or succession timing; the age guideline is the only formal refresh mechanism and it is being waived for two members.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own stated age-75 guideline (applied to Al Gore after 21 years and James Bell after 9 years in 2024) is the relevant base rate, not an external norm.
rows.weakens: 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025 and 7 of 8 directors are independent, so holders are not signalling discontent; the guideline says 'generally', which permits exceptions.
rows.implication: Governance is stable but weakly refreshed; an investor should price a slower correction if AI-era capital allocation goes wrong, and should not pay a governance premium.
rows.confidence: high - names, ages, start years and the guideline are in the 2026 proxy.
rows.follow_up: Did the board formally waive the age guideline for Levinson and Sugar, and who chairs the board after 2027?

rows.finding: FY2025 returned $106.1bn to shareholders ($90.7bn buybacks plus $15.4bn dividends) against free cash flow of $98.8bn, i.e. 107% of FCF, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%.
rows.mechanism: Buybacks shrink the denominator (diluted shares fell 6.9% from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026) and a lower tax rate lifts the numerator, so reported EPS growth overstates operating growth; the equity behaves partly as a bond-like cash-return instrument.
rows.benchmark: Company's own FY2023-FY2025 buybacks of $263.2bn and its FY2024 effective tax rate of 24.1% provide the counterfactual.
rows.weakens: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% with a 50.1% gross margin including a ~2pp tariff-refund benefit, so operating momentum in FY2026 is genuine and the 'financial engineering' charge is weaker for the current year.
rows.implication: Underwrite the holding on operating growth and cash conversion, not on EPS optics; if buybacks slow, headline EPS growth converges to operating growth.
rows.confidence: high - all figures from the FY2025 statements and the Q3 FY2026 exhibit 99.1.
rows.follow_up: What is the FY2026 buyback pace after the $100bn May 2025 authorisation, and how much of FY2025 EPS growth was tax?

rows.finding: Two Irish subsidiaries' Irish branches received tax opinions in 1991 and 2007 allocating profits; the Commission's 2016-08-30 decision was annulled by the General Court on 2020-07-15 but confirmed by the ECJ on 2024-09-10, producing a one-time $10.2bn net tax charge in Q4 FY2024 and $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow.
rows.mechanism: The entity map's profit allocation, not its legal ownership, was the source of the tax advantage; Irish law changed from January 2015 and the ECJ judgment converted a contingent liability into a paid one, so the post-2015 structure is taxed on a permanently less favourable basis.
rows.benchmark: Effective tax rate of 24.1% in FY2024 versus 15.6% in FY2025 shows how much of the reported rate is discrete items rather than structure.
rows.weakens: The FY2025 rate of 15.6% shows the rate can still fall on discrete benefits, so the direction of travel is not monotonic.
rows.implication: The Irish tax leg of the compounding story is over; model a mid-to-high teens effective rate rather than historical single-digit foreign rates, and treat further EU tax integration as a live risk.
rows.confidence: high - the 10-K note states the dates, amounts and offsets.
rows.follow_up: What is the FY2026 effective rate excluding discrete items, and where is residual non-US IP now booked?

rows.finding: The Services line that carries the highest margin (75.4% gross margin in FY2025 versus 36.8% for products) is the one attacked by live proceedings: the DOJ monopolisation suit filed 2024-03-21, a EUR 500m DMA fine and cease-and-desist on 2025-04-23 with a second Article 6(4) file open, and an Epic contempt finding on 2025-04-30 referred to the US Attorney.
rows.mechanism: Remedies target the commission and anti-steering rules that let Apple tax third-party distribution, so they attack the rent, not the product; a structural remedy would compress the 75% margin line while leaving hardware intact.
rows.benchmark: Services gross margin 75.4% against products 36.8% in FY2025 quantifies the rent at stake.
rows.weakens: Services revenue still grew 14.1% in the nine months to 2026-06-27 while these cases were live, so remedies have not yet dented growth.
rows.implication: The highest-margin revenue stream carries the largest legal tail; that, not hardware competition, is the reason to demand a discount to a pure compounder multiple.
rows.confidence: medium-high - case facts are from the 10-K; the revenue effect is inferred from segment growth.
rows.follow_up: What Services revenue is directly exposed to US third-party payment rules, and what is the appeal timetable in the Ninth Circuit?

rows.finding: Twelve months of Form 4s to 2026-10-29 show no purchases and 46 sales of 687,127 shares for $208.0m, led by director Levinson ($86.7m, not under a 10b5-1 plan) and Tim Cook ($80.4m); Cook's disclosed holding of 3,280,295 shares is 0.02% of the company but about $1.09bn at the $332.94 price of his 2026-10-02 sale.
rows.mechanism: At a $3.8trn market capitalisation, percentage ownership is a poor measure of alignment; dollar exposure and unvested RSUs are what bind management, and planned sales under 10b5-1 rules carry little information.
rows.benchmark: The company's own requirement that the CEO hold ten times base salary ($30m against a $3m salary) is the alignment test management sets for itself.
rows.weakens: All but three of the sales were 10b5-1 planned and three were gifts, so the pattern is scheduled diversification, not a signal of inside information.
rows.implication: Alignment is adequate in dollars and weak in votes, so the investor should watch changes in unvested equity and retention terms rather than the percentage table.
rows.confidence: high for the trades; medium for the dollar value of Cook's stake, which is a calculation across two sources.
rows.follow_up: What are the retention and vesting terms offered to Ternus on appointment, and does Cook's executive-chair role carry new equity?

plan.decision_question: Is Apple's legal, ownership and governance structure clean and stable enough to underwrite a multi-year holding?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years - one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit - but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit past its own age-75 rule, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality.
plan.why_different: This section owns identity, legal structure, ownership and board mechanics; the business model and unit economics belong to the financial sections, the product roadmap to the product section, and litigation substance to the regulatory section.
plan.mechanism: One share class removes control risk but concentrates governance in a long-tenured board; capital return plus a falling tax rate flattered EPS while the Irish profit-allocation structure that supported the tax rate was closed by the ECJ; the highest-margin revenue line is the one exposed to antitrust remedies.
plan.comparison_set: Alphabet as the multi-class mega-cap peer; Apple's own 2011-2026 record (cumulative TSR +2,162% under Cook) as the base rate for a leadership handover; Apple's stated age-75 board policy applied to its 2024 retirements.
plan.counter_evidence: 92% say-on-pay support, seven of eight directors independent, Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 16% and gross margin of 50.1%, and a CEO whose disclosed stake is worth about $1.09bn all argue the governance and alignment discount should be small.
plan.visual: KPI table (share structure, float, independence, tenure, capital return, tax rate, iPhone concentration) with the entity table and the dated timeline.
plan.prohibited: clean structure as an assertion without evidence, strong governance, well positioned, stable leadership, huge market, risks are manageable, any sentence about how the report was written

rows.finding: On 2026-04-17 the board appointed John Ternus (50 at appointment) CEO effective 2026-09-01; he joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became a vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and SVP in 2021, and holds a 1997 Penn degree in mechanical engineering and applied mechanics; Cook becomes Executive Chair and Levinson Lead Independent Director.
rows.mechanism: Promoting the hardware engineering head keeps the integrated product model intact but transfers the CEO role from a commercial operator who built the China supply chain and services pricing to an engineer whose record is product development.
rows.benchmark: Apple's own 2011 handover, when an operations executive with 13 years as COO replaced a product founder; and Microsoft's internal CEO succession as the peer base rate for continuity.
rows.weakens: Ternus has run the largest product organisation at Apple for five years, which is broader than the title suggests; internal promotion is also the pattern that worked in 2011.
rows.implication: Continuity is high and the product-integration model is safe, but the skills most tested in 2026-28 (AI platform economics, regulatory negotiation, tariffs) are not the ones on his record, which argues for a wait-for-evidence stance rather than paying a new-CEO premium.

rows.follow_up: What operating scope has Ternus had outside hardware engineering, and does his employment agreement disclose a retention award?

rows.finding: On 2025-12-01 Apple announced John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, with Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety moved into the software organisation, and the rest of the AI org split between Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue.
rows.mechanism: AI accountability was spread across a standalone SVP, the software org and the operations org; folding models and safety under Software Engineering shortens the path from model to product but leaves the P&L owner for AI undisclosed.
rows.benchmark: Q3 FY2026 revenue growth of 16% and the July 2026 statement that Siri AI shipped at WWDC26 are the test of whether the reorganisation delivered.
rows.weakens: Apple shipped the all-new Siri AI by WWDC26, so the reorganisation produced a deliverable within seven months; the delay that triggered it is not quantified in any filing.
rows.implication: Treat AI execution as an unresolved item requiring a milestone (shipped Siri AI adoption and a disclosed AI roadmap) before adding to a position.
rows.confidence: high on the reorganisation; medium on whether accountability is now clear, which the company has not disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Who now owns Siri roadmap and model strategy, and does Subramanya report to the CEO or only to Federighi?

rows.finding: On 2025-12-06 it was reported that Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, told Tim Cook he was seriously considering leaving the company; no departure or new role has been disclosed in any filing since.
rows.mechanism: Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and hardware margin; losing the executive who built it threatens a multi-year roadmap that competitors cannot copy quickly.
rows.benchmark: Products gross margin of 36.8% in FY2025 rests on custom silicon and is the line at risk if silicon leadership weakens.
rows.weakens: The report is unconfirmed and Apple has disclosed no change; promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be exactly the move that retains silicon talent.
rows.implication: This is the single most underpriced key-person risk in the holding; ask for the retention arrangement before sizing a position.
rows.confidence: medium - single media report, denied by nobody and confirmed by nobody; no departure has been disclosed.
rows.follow_up: Has Srouji been given a new title, retention award or CTO role, and who is his designated successor?

rows.finding: Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m (base $3m unchanged since 2016, target cash $6m, target equity $50m, 75% performance-based); the other named executive officers each target about $23m (base $1m, 200% cash target, $20m equity); Parekh's CFO package was $1m base with 175% cash target and $16.75m target equity.
rows.mechanism: Apple pays small annual awards with long vesting (about 4.5 years) and no employment contracts, so retention depends on unvested equity rather than contractual protection; peers use front-loaded mega-grants that make leaving expensive.
rows.benchmark: Microsoft's Nadella at $96.5m reported for FY2025 and Alphabet's Pichai at $10.9m reported for 2025 but with a 2026 target equity award of $210m and a 1.35m-share PSU vesting in February 2026.
rows.weakens: Pay follows performance: 92% say-on-pay in 2025 and a 2,162% cumulative TSR from 2011 to 2025 make the structure defensible, and unvested RSUs are large in absolute terms.
rows.implication: Shareholders get a chief executive paid well below mega-cap peers, which is a real plus, but the same restraint applied to undisclosed SVPs is a poaching risk in the AI labour market.
rows.confidence: high on Apple's numbers; medium on peers, where one figure comes from reporting rather than the proxy itself.
rows.follow_up: What are the 2026 awards to Ternus and to the non-NEO SVPs, and do they include multi-year retention grants?

rows.finding: Apple's Section 16 population is narrow: the Form 4 filers in the twelve months to 2026-10-29 are Cook (now Executive Chair), Ternus, O'Brien, Parekh, Newstead, principal accounting officer Borders and director Levinson; Craig Federighi, Eddy Cue, Johny Srouji and Greg Joswiak do not appear, so their ownership and trades are not publicly disclosed.
rows.mechanism: Non-disclosure of the operating bench means outside holders cannot price succession, retention or internal competition for the CEO role from filings alone.
rows.benchmark: The 2026 proxy names only six named executive officers and four current executives in the ownership table, against a peer group whose CEOs are covered individually in sector research.
rows.weakens: The named group still covers operations, finance, legal and retail, i.e. every function with external reporting exposure, so the disclosure gap is about product and technology leaders rather than the whole bench.
rows.implication: Information asymmetry is material for a people-dependent thesis; the report should carry an explicit disclosure limitation and the investor should seek management access before sizing.
rows.confidence: high - the set of filers and titles comes from the Form 4 list itself.
rows.follow_up: Will Apple designate its AI and silicon leaders as Section 16 officers, and what does the 2027 proxy disclose about their awards?

rows.finding: In roughly eighteen months Apple changed CFO (Parekh, 2025-01-01), COO (Khan, 2025), general counsel (Newstead from 2026-03-01, with Adams moving to government affairs until retirement in late 2026), lost its AI chief (2025-12-01) and its environment chief (Lisa Jackson, announced 2025-12-04), and named a new CEO (2026-09-01).
rows.mechanism: Simultaneous turnover in finance, operations, legal, environment and AI removes institutional knowledge at the moment the company must re-price its services rent and defend antitrust cases.
rows.benchmark: Apple's 2011 transition had one CEO change with no simultaneous CFO, COO, GC or AI-lead change.
rows.weakens: Apple describes each move as a planned transition, the CFO and COO successors were internal, and there is no filing evidence of dispute or dysfunction.
rows.implication: A cluster of senior turnover into a CEO change raises execution risk; it supports a conditions-based entry rather than buying the transition narrative.
rows.confidence: high on dates and roles; the causation between turnover and execution is an interpretation.
rows.follow_up: Which of these roles is now filled by an external hire, and what is the average tenure of the current executive team?

plan.thesis_sentence: The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era - hardware, operations, finance - and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation after the Siri delay, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition.

plan.mechanism: Apple built its moat on integrated hardware and a distribution rent; the AI transition shifts value to models, data and cloud, where Apple's bench is thinnest. Its pay model (annual, modest, at-will, heavy unvested RSUs) retains people who value stability but leaves non-disclosed SVPs exposed to poaching, and the 2025-26 turnover cluster removes the executives who held the China supply chain, the legal fights and the AI org.

rows.finding: The June 2026 quarter's 50.1% gross margin included 2 points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS; TrendForce projects 4Q26 conventional DRAM contract prices +10-15% QoQ and NAND +15-20%, with DRAM tight into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A cost shock hits a hardware line priced months ahead: Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, so the gross margin absorbs the increase before any price offset arrives.
rows.benchmark: iPhone 18 Pro BOM +38% YoY with memory 34% of BOM against ~10% a year earlier; 200bp of gross margin = $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of trailing $8.72.
rows.weakens: Q4 guidance of 47-48% reported already assumes part of the increase, and memory price growth is moderating from the 146% first-quarter 2026 jump; services at 76.3% margin cushion the blend.
rows.implication: A 46% gross margin takes FY2027 EPS to about $9.3 and, at 29x, fair value to $270 - the entry price becomes the base case, not the bear case.
rows.confidence: high on the cost data, medium on the pass-through because Apple's price elasticity is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What gross margin does management guide for the December 2026 quarter, and how much FY2027 memory is contracted at fixed prices?

rows.finding: The trial record put the Google payment at $20bn in 2022, 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income at near-pure margin; the district court remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the D.C. Circuit appeal No. 26-5023 with a DOJ cross-appeal seeking a ban is live into 2027.
rows.mechanism: A rent with almost no marginal cost is capitalised in the services multiple; a ban removes operating income and de-rates the line that carries most of the terminal value.
rows.benchmark: A ban is -10% to -13% of EPS and, at 30-35x, -$35 to -$45 a share; a lower rate is the more likely outcome and is worth less than the market's implied perpetuity.
rows.weakens: The payment survived the district court remedy, Apple has filed in support of it, and appellate courts defer on remedies; the 2022 figure may understate or overstate the 2026 rate.
rows.implication: Price a 20-25% probability of loss into any entry; do not pay a services multiple on the full toll.
rows.confidence: medium: the legal record is high-confidence, the outcome and the payment's current size are not
rows.follow_up: What is the current annual payment and term, and when is the D.C. Circuit argument scheduled?

rows.finding: From 2026-10-01 Apple's EU terms charge 26% on in-app purchase, 20% on alternative payment, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission; Europe was 26.7% of nine-month FY2026 revenue.
rows.mechanism: Regulated take-rate compression on the highest-margin line transfers rent to developers and alternative storefronts and lowers switching costs out of the App Store.
rows.benchmark: EU band of 5-26% against 15-30% elsewhere; each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple retains 26% on in-app purchase; EU App Store revenue is not disclosed and the direct hit may be 1-2% of operating income.
rows.implication: The EU amount is manageable; the template is not. Underwrite services growth at 10-12%, not 15%, and treat a US move to a 5-15% band as the bear case.
rows.confidence: medium: the fee schedule is high-confidence, the revenue exposure is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: How much EU App Store commission revenue is at stake, and how fast are developers migrating to external distribution?

rows.finding: Apple trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median and a 31.0x four-year mean, while the DCF is $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity and $193 at 9.5%.
rows.mechanism: Almost all of the value is terminal, so the discount rate and the exit multiple dominate: each 50bp on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%.
rows.benchmark: Reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%; the 52-week low of $243.42 is a 29.4% drawdown.
rows.weakens: Forward 35.2x equals the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and quality franchises have held premium multiples through a 4.93% ten-year Treasury.
rows.implication: Zero position at $344.63; a starter only at $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% across 27-34x exits.
rows.confidence: high on the arithmetic, medium on the timing of any re-rating
rows.follow_up: What would the ten-year yield have to do for a 7.0% cost of equity to be defensible, and how sticky is the passive bid?

rows.finding: China shipments fell 10% YoY in Q3 2026 on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share in the quarter, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in H2 2026.
rows.mechanism: A shrinking unit pool with a fixed premium layer means revenue growth comes from price and share, both of which reverse when demand is pulled forward.
rows.benchmark: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; Apple grew 30% in the nine months against a market down 4.3% in Q2 2026.
rows.weakens: Apple gained share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor; the two trackers disagree by 1.7 points on Apple's Q3 share, so the data are noisy.
rows.implication: Do not capitalise the 30% China growth; a 20% China decline is about 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS.
rows.confidence: medium-high on the direction, medium on the magnitude because the trackers disagree
rows.follow_up: What share of the China growth was pull-forward ahead of Apple's H2 2026 price rises?

rows.finding: Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14 on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capex fell to $6.80bn; no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation.
rows.mechanism: Rented intelligence is operating expense with no asset behind it: the marginal AI dollar is a margin cost, and the supplier also owns Android, so renewal terms carry the bargaining power.
rows.benchmark: A $1bn licence is 0.6% of trailing operating income; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would be several times that and would land in the 76.3% services margin.
rows.weakens: Apple keeps distribution, personal context and Private Cloud Compute, and a better assistant may sell handsets even if Apple does not own the model.
rows.implication: Treat AI as a cost line, not a moat; the upgrade cycle must show up in units and ASP before it is worth paying for.
rows.confidence: low-to-medium: the licence price is reported, not confirmed, and the AI P&L structure is an absence of disclosure
rows.follow_up: What are the Gemini renewal terms, and who signs off the AI budget?

rows.finding: Trailing free cash flow of $136.7bn includes $14.1bn from a rise in other liabilities; normalised FCF is $122.6-125.1bn, while intangibles rose $12.1bn in nine months and inventory is $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end.
rows.mechanism: Working-capital accruals and acquisitions convert into free cash flow without being earnings; inventory build is the channel through which a demand miss becomes a write-down.
rows.benchmark: Conversion of 0.95-0.97x normalised against 1.06x headline, still ahead of Microsoft at 0.50x; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of trailing operating income.
rows.weakens: Apple's cash conversion is genuinely better than peers and the liability swing may be a timing item that reverses as memory is pre-bought.
rows.implication: Use the normalised $122.6-125.1bn for valuation; a 30% lower FCF of $95.7bn no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback plus dividends.
rows.confidence: medium: the swing is filed, its cause is not disclosed
rows.follow_up: What is acquired for $12.1bn of net intangibles, and what sits in the $13.5bn rise in other non-current liabilities?

rows.finding: The board waived its age-75 guideline for Levinson (75) and Sugar (77); from 2026-09-01 Apple has nine directors, two non-independent, with Cook Executive Chair. Srouji was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20, superseding the December 2025 departure report. FY2025 returned $106.1bn, 107% of $98.8bn FCF but 93% of the $114.6bn normalised for the Irish tax payment.
rows.mechanism: Key-person and board-refresh risk affects the roadmap rather than the near-term cash flow; capital return is sustainable on normalised cash but not on the depressed FY2025 figure.
rows.benchmark: 92% say-on-pay, no dual-class stock, internal CFO and COO promotions; underlying FY2025 EPS growth of about 10.6% once the prior year's $10.2bn tax charge is added back, not the 22.7% headline.

plan.decision_question: At what entry price do the memory, search-payment, DMA and China risks still leave a long-only fund a 9% three-year return, and which signpost would invalidate that entry?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63.
plan.why_different: This is the only section that prices the left tail and the multiple: it separates fatal risks from execution risks, stress-tests the base case against smaller markets, lower FCF and higher discount rates, and gives each risk a dated signpost.
plan.mechanism: Each risk transmits to value through one of two channels: a cost shock against a 48.7% gross margin that applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, or a legal remedy against two near-pure-margin services tolls, and a 39.5x multiple capitalises both at a 2.5% earnings yield so either shock is amplified by the exit multiple.
plan.comparison_set: Peer median 20.2x P/E against Apple's 39.5x; Apple's own four-year mean 31.0x and FY2022 trough 24.6x; the $243.42 52-week low (-29.4%); Samsung's mobile division losing KRW0.8tn and Xiaomi at an 8.5% handset margin show what the memory shock does to weaker hardware models.

rows.weakens: Cisco peaked at 201x earnings; Apple is at 39.5x, an order of magnitude cheaper, so the same outcome needs a far larger de-rating.
rows.implication: Base the valuation on multiple mean reversion, not on growth; the exit multiple, not the business, sets the three-year return.
rows.confidence: high on the fact, medium on the analogy.
rows.follow_up: What multiple does Apple hold if revenue growth settles at 5% and the buyback continues at $80bn a year?

rows.finding: The S&P 500 is at 7,580.07, up 10.7% year to date and 3.4% below its high; the Nasdaq is 8.2% below its high; the VIX is 19.42 at the 77th percentile; the 10-year Treasury yields 4.93% [S8, S18, S9, S10].
rows.mechanism: A 4.93% risk-free rate anchors the cost of equity at 9%, and technology is down 8.3% over one month against SPY down 0.9%, so the sector is being de-rated while the index holds.
rows.benchmark: Apple's DCF uses a 9.0% cost of equity; the current price implies 7.0%.
rows.weakens: The index is near its high and breadth can carry a mega-cap through a sector rotation.
rows.implication: Do not underwrite multiple expansion; demand a discount to intrinsic value before buying.
rows.confidence: high — timestamped market data.
rows.follow_up: Does the 10-year yield break 5%, and does technology keep underperforming into the December quarter?

rows.finding: The franchise's primary numbers: TTM revenue $466,823M, gross profit $227,123M, net income $128,930M, with services at 25.8% of revenue and 40.3% of gross profit [S6].
rows.mechanism: A 76.3% services margin on a 25.8% revenue share supplies the gross profit that funds R&D 2.1 times over, which is why the multiple has always been a services multiple rather than a hardware one.
rows.benchmark: Product gross margin 40.1% in Q3 FY2026 against services 76.3%.
rows.weakens: Services fell to 25.2% of revenue from 26.2% as iPhone grew faster, the first mix decline since at least FY2023.
rows.implication: Own the quality but price it off services, which is exactly where the regulatory risk sits.
rows.confidence: high — filed figures.
rows.follow_up: What is the services gross margin once the EU fee schedule and the search payment are renegotiated?

plan.decision_question: Does AAPL belong on a long-only fund's watchlist, and at what price and with what conditions does it become an actionable long?
plan.thesis_sentence: Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one: the franchise earns a premium multiple, but at $344.63 the shares already discount the AI cycle, the buyback and a regulatory clean sweep, so the decision is to watch and buy near $270, not to own today.
plan.why_different: The analyst sections describe the business; this section prices the decision, tests it against three analogs and fixes the entry, the size and the sell trigger.
plan.mechanism: Three-year return = EPS growth of 8-11% plus a 2.4-point buyback tailwind plus the change in the multiple; at 35.2x forward the multiple must fall unless growth beats, and the analog base rate says the multiple does the damage.
plan.comparison_set: S&P 500 at 18.09x forward; Apple's own 12-month average of 35.66x and four-year mean of 31.0x; Microsoft 1998-2001, Nokia 2007-2013, Cisco 2000-2025.
plan.counter_evidence: A D.C. Circuit ban on the search payment, a 46% gross margin on memory costs, or an AI upgrade cycle that lifts units would each move value toward the bear or bull case, and the multiple could stay at 35x for years.
plan.visual: The scenarios component carries Bull, Base and Bear with probabilities; the analogs component carries the three decision rules.
plan.prohibited: huge market, strong team, high barriers to entry, clear business model, fierce competition, risks are manageable, well positioned, recently, many, about N; any sentence about how the section is written.

thesis.author: Lead Analyst

spines.spine: Public equity — earnings quality, competitive position, valuation, catalysts, downside risk
spines.must_answer: Is the market mispricing Apple's future cash flow or its risk? Framed on FY2025/FY2026 revenue growth, services mix, gross margin, FCF conversion, ROIC versus WACC, the multiple versus peers and its own history, the catalyst calendar (iPhone cycle, Apple Intelligence, capital return) and the bear-case drawdown. Answered: the franchise compounds but the price already capitalises a 50.1% peak margin and a 35.2x forward multiple; DCF $212, base $284, probability-weighted $292 against $344.63.

spines.spine: Policy / geopolitics-sensitive — national strategy, export controls, tariffs, platform regulation, market access
spines.must_answer: Does policy create a moat or a hidden constraint? Quantified: the ~$20bn Google default-search payment (18.3% of services revenue, 15% of operating income, a 2022 litigated estimate), the EU 5-26% fee schedule in force 2026-10-01, DOJ v Apple filed 2024-03-21 with no trial date, the Ninth Circuit contempt of 2025-12-11 and Supreme Court certiorari granted 2026-06-30, and tariffs that add two points of gross margin in refunds while memory costs rise.

spines.spine: Consumer / brand — demand durability versus promotion-driven demand
spines.must_answer: Is iPhone and services demand durable? Tested replacement-cycle length, installed-base growth and switching costs, services attach and pricing power, Greater China demand and Huawei, and whether growth is unit-driven or price/mix-driven. Answered: FY2026 growth is price and mix (units down 16.7% in a market up 6.3% in value), iPhone +22.4% in nine months against services +14.1%, and China is a shrinking pool where Apple gained 4.8 points of share.

research_plan.industry_map: Consumer electronics plus digital services. Value chain: in-house silicon and OS design (Apple) → foundry and memory (TSMC and others) → components and displays → contract assembly (Foxconn, Pegatron, Luxshare; China with an India/Vietnam shift) → distribution (carriers, Apple retail, e-commerce) → an installed base of active devices → platform (iOS/macOS/watchOS) → services (App Store, iCloud, advertising, subscriptions, AppleCare, payments). Decisive bottleneck: control of the OS and installed base that converts hardware gross margin into recurring, higher-margin services revenue; that bottleneck is now squeezed by platform regulation (EU DMA, US App Store remedies) and by the AI capability race that determines the next upgrade cycle. Apple sits as the orchestrator: design and platform in-house, manufacturing outsourced, distribution partly owned, services attached to its own base.
research_plan.geo_lens: Material. Map five reporting regions — Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia Pacific — for revenue, margin and growth; map the manufacturing footprint (China, India, Vietnam) and the supplier base (Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, US); map capital markets (Nasdaq listing, USD reporting) and the comparable set (US mega-cap technology plus global handset makers). Greater China is the swing geography for both demand and supply-chain risk: 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, a market down 10% on Counterpoint and 15.4% on IDC in Q3 2026, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%.
research_plan.policy_lens: Material. Jurisdictions mapped: United States (tariffs and Section 232 semiconductor/consumer-electronics actions, DOJ antitrust case against Apple, the Google default-search payment, export controls on advanced chips); European Union (Digital Markets Act fee schedule from 2026-10-01 at 5-26%, the EUR500M DMA fine of 2025-04-23, interoperability obligations, the General Court's 2026-07-08 ruling); China (market access, local-content and security rules, Huawei competition, rare-earth and export-control leverage); India (production-linked incentives that expired 2026-03-31, manufacturing shift); United Kingdom (CMA mobile-market investigation). Policy hits both revenue (App Store take rate, default payments) and cost (tariffs, supply-chain relocation, memory).

research_plan.hypothesis: Watchlist, not ownership, at $344.63 on 2026-10-30. Apple is a genuine cash compounder — 0.97x normalised cash conversion on $125.1bn, $62.2bn of net cash, services at 40.3% of gross profit — but the price capitalises a peak margin and a peak multiple: DCF $212 at a 9.0% cost of equity, sum of the parts $177-238, base case $284, probability-weighted value $292. It becomes an actionable long through a staged entry: 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270, a second tranche at $245, the 5% cap below $225, and a stop-review above $380. The two facts that would change the call are a 46% gross margin and a D.C. Circuit ban on the Google search payment.

items: Use web and data tools for fresh facts whenever a company, market, price, policy, filing, funding, or executive fact may have changed.
For each major section, record targeted search strings, opened sources, source IDs, and why the selected sources are decision-grade rather than merely convenient.
Use the server's checks for deterministic QA, extraction, citation checks and the delivery folder; do not rely on a one-shot narrative draft.
Do not generate repeated filler paragraphs such as per-section original-document priority, citation-anchor blocks, or repeated metric-card copy; each section must contain content-specific analysis.
Before drafting, write a section distinctness plan: the unique decision question, mechanism, comparison set, counter-evidence, and best visual artifact for each section.
For each section, draft one final-report thesis sentence that directly analyzes the company; never copy internal plan labels or rubric language into the report.
Remove repeated visible scaffolds such as "Economic mechanism", "Comparison and benchmark", "Counter-evidence and risk" and "Investor implication"; keep the scaffold internal.
Use a verdict strip, compact decision cards, selected tables, and at most a few KPI strips; do not repeat the same card, grid or dashboard pattern in every section.
Before writing the executive briefing, summarize the non-consensus or consensus view and the exact evidence that changes the decision.
Treat OCR as a pipeline: inventory files, OCR scan- or slide-heavy material, and keep page, slide or table references for every extracted claim.
Check every page holding numbers, TAM, valuation, customers, clinical or regulatory claims, policy claims, financing terms or team credentials before relying on it.
Mark OCR-derived claims low confidence until checked or corroborated; use ranges for OCR-derived financial inputs.
Build a claim verification table for material company-provided claims: verified, partially verified, unverified, contradicted, or not publicly disclosed.
profile_requirements.evidence: Completed across the run. Fresh facts: the team pulled Apple's FY2025 10-K, the 10-Q for the quarter ended 2026-06-27, the 2026 proxy and 8-Ks from SEC EDGAR [S5, S6, S11, S56], timestamped market data at $344.63 on 2026-10-30 20:00 UTC [S97], the market regime (S&P 500 7,580.07, VIX 19.42 at the 77th percentile, ten-year 4.93%) [S9, S10], and dated regulatory records: the EU DMA fee schedule and EUR500M fine [S77], the D.C. District remedy of 2025-12-05 and the D.C. Circuit appeal No. 26-5023 [S70, S76], the Ninth Circuit contempt of 2025-12-11 and Supreme Court certiorari of 2026-06-30 [S79]. Source register: 147 sources with type, date, confidence and claims, cited by visible [S#] IDs in every section; each section's evidence block records its targeted queries and why each source is decision-grade. Section distinctness: every evidence block carries a plan with the unique decision question, mechanism, comparison set, counter-evidence, best visual, thesis sentence and what makes the section different; sections were checked to remove scaffold labels and repeated card patterns. Evidence matrix: all fourteen sections carry an evidence block with its gate passed (two independent sources, a primary or near-primary source, two numeric facts or a missing-data note, mechanism, comparison, counter-evidence, investor implication, diligence questions). OCR: no client documents were attached and no scanned or slide-heavy material entered the report, so the OCR pipeline and low-confidence OCR rules have no items to apply; no claim in the report rests on OCR text. Company claims: material company-provided claims carry a status label — the 2.5bn installed base, the ~$1bn Gemini licence, the Siri and Private Cloud Compute capability claims and the $1.4tn ecosystem are marked unverified or reported-not-confirmed, and the product section's patent table is marked low confidence. Red-team pass: completed and filed, section 10 written, and five cross-section corrections pushed to their owners. Gaps: seven user data requests filed for records behind logins or paywalls, and the FY2026 10-K is not due until results on 2026-11-02.
