### The margin is the record, and part of it was purchased

Gross margin went from 44.1% in FY2023 to 46.2%, 46.9%, 49.1% in the nine months of FY2026 and 48.7% trailing, and the June 2026 quarter printed 50.1%, a record. Services, at a 76.3% gross margin, are 40.3% of the gross-profit pool on 25.8% of revenue; products are not. Products gross margin rose to 39.9% from 36.9% on product mix and tariff refunds, and the 30 July 2026 release attributes 2 points of the quarter's gross margin and $0.11 of its $2.02 EPS to them. The cost side has turned: memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average and the 10-Q expects the component trends "to intensify". A 47-48% gross margin, not 50.1%, is the level to capitalise. [S17, S68]

::: info warning
**Two percentage points of the record 50.1% gross margin are a one-off tariff refund, and the memory cycle is turning against the hardware line (S6, S17).**

The release puts the refund at 2 points of gross margin and $0.11 of the $2.02 quarterly EPS (S17); products gross margin of 39.9% compares with 36.9%, and memory prices rose 146% with the 10-Q warning that cost pressure will intensify (S6, S68). Two hundred basis points off trailing gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, or 6.0% of $8.72.
:::

### Cash conversion is real, but a liability accrual did the lifting

Nine-month operating cash flow rose $35,242M to $116,996M while net income rose $16,920M: non-cash add-backs added $1,956M more and working capital $16,366M more. The dominant line is other current and non-current liabilities, +$10,016M against −$15,161M a year earlier. Other non-current liabilities rose $13,531M to $55,080M while other current liabilities fell $4,128M to $62,259M, a combined $9,403M build that reconciles to the cash line within $613M; the prior year carries the ~$15.8B Irish State Aid settlement (cash taxes paid of $37,332M against a $15,381M provision), with the $15,552M added in FY2024 within $250M of the $15.8B payable. The line's clean history is $3,031M in FY2023, −$248M in FY2024 and $4,724M in FY2025, a $2,502M average, so the $14,101M it puts into trailing free cash flow is the soft spot. The $13,270M of gross intangibles added against investing "other" of only $1,780M is consistent with the $13,531M build being deferred consideration — an unpaid purchase, which would make $123,152M the figure, inside the band. competition.author: Market Analyst
competition.markdown:
Apple is winning the competition for profit and price while ceding unit share in China: it holds 65% of premium phone units and a 40% product gross margin, but Huawei is taking premium share in a shrinking China market and regulation is capping the services take rate, so its competitive position is strengthening in hardware, holding in services and weakening at the margin in China. Apple's own 10-K concedes a minority share in smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables and says some of its markets have experienced little or no growth; the useful analysis is therefore per product, because the iPhone, Mac, wearables and services each face a different rival set [S5].

| Competitor | Product | Technology | Regulatory status | Performance | Price | Share | Strengths vs Apple | Weaknesses vs Apple | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Samsung | Galaxy S26, Z Fold 7 | Android; Exynos 2600 or Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 | Unrestricted | Flagship parity; foldable incumbent | Premium | 19% global 2025; 23% in Q3 2026 | Foldable head start; carrier breadth | MX division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 | S91, S92, S120 |
| Huawei | Mate and Pura; HarmonyOS | Kirin silicon; HarmonyOS | China scale; US export restrictions | Premium camera and battery | Premium | 22.6% China in Q2 2026 | Domestic supply chain; holds prices | Little share outside China | S87, S86 |
| Xiaomi | Xiaomi 17 series | Android; Snapdragon | Unrestricted | Value flagship | Mid-premium | 11.5% global in Q2 2026 | Price-performance; AIoT and EV ecosystem | 8.5% handset gross margin; profit -42.6% | S90 |
| Google | Pixel 11 | Android; Tensor; Gemini | Unrestricted | AI-first software | Premium | Not disclosed | Gemini integration; search distribution | Small hardware distribution | S15, S50 |
| Lenovo, HP, Dell | PC lines | Windows on x86 | Unrestricted | Enterprise and channel strength | $600-2,000 | 24.4%, 19.1%, 13.6% in Q2 2026 | Enterprise channel; price tiers | No in-house OS-silicon integration | S95 |
| Spotify | Music streaming and app distribution | App; DMA alternative distribution | EU DMA beneficiary | 300M paying subscribers | Subscription | Twice Apple Music's subscriber base | Cross-platform; podcasts | No hardware bundle | S93, S77 |
| Alphabet | Search, YouTube, Play | Android; Gemini | Antitrust scrutiny | Advertising scale | Ad-funded | $471B TTM revenue | Search and advertising scale | AI capex dilution | S15, S50 |
| Status quo | Longer device life, refurbished | None | None | Adequate for most users | Zero | Not disclosed | Free and familiar | No new capability | S87 |

Huawei is the most dangerous competitor to Apple's profit pool, and Samsung is the most dangerous to its unit position [S87, S86, S91, S92, S84]. Huawei led China with 22.6% in Q2 2026 against Apple's 18.1%, after its highest share since Q4 2020 in the prior quarter, and IDC expects HarmonyOS shipments to nearly triple to 51M units in 2026; Huawei funds that push with CNY192.3B of R&D, 21.8% of CNY880.9B of 2025 revenue. Samsung is broader, with 19% global share in 2025 and 23% in Q3 2026, a foldable incumbent and the only rival with scale across phones, wearables and PCs, but its MX and Networks division lost KRW0.6T in Q3 2026 despite 10.55% revenue growth, so it cannot buy share indefinitely. Huawei takes price and profit; Samsung takes volume and loses money doing it.

Share trends from 2025 to 2026 show Apple gaining value and premium ground while its unit share moves sideways [S92, S120, S94, S84, S17]. Apple led 2025 with 20% of global units and 10% growth and Samsung followed at 19%; in Q3 2026 Samsung held 23% to Apple's 22% as the market fell 20%. The premium layer is where Apple's position improves: its 65% of $600-plus units in H1 2026 came with 9% growth, and IDC expects iOS to reach a record 23.6% share in 2026. Pricing power shows in the gross margin, 40.1% on products in Q3 FY2026 versus 34.5% a year earlier, with iPhone revenue up 22% in nine months. The caveat is that the price increase is imposed by a memory shock rather than earned by innovation alone: NAND and DRAM costs are up more than 300%, and Apple's signalling of further rises pulled Chinese demand forward.

China is the one region where the competitive position is deteriorating on share even as revenue rises [S87, S6, S86]. Apple's Greater China revenue grew 30% in the first nine months of FY2026, but that came against a market down 4.2% in H1 2026 and with Apple at 18.1% share to Huawei's 22.6%; Huawei grew 19.4% and Apple 24.4% in Q2 2026, both by holding prices while OPPO, vivo and Xiaomi raised theirs and lost 9.7%, 11.4% and 21.7% respectively. The top six vendors hold 96% of the market, so the fight is for premium share inside a contracting pool, and Huawei's HarmonyOS scale gives it a domestic platform Apple cannot match on localisation. Apple's revenue growth is a price-hold plus pull-forward effect, not evidence that it has regained structural leadership in China.

Regulation is now a competitive force that transfers rent from Apple to its rivals [S77, S102, S93]. From 1 October 2026 the EU applies a 26% commission on App Store in-app purchases, 20% on alternative payment processing, 15% on link-outs and a 5% Core Technology Commission on apps distributed through alternative marketplaces or the web, after Apple was fined EUR500M for DMA non-compliance in 2025. The practical effect is to lower switching costs out of the App Store in a region that is 26.7% of Apple's revenue and to hand Spotify, Epic and alternative storefronts a distribution channel on iOS; Spotify already has 300M paying subscribers against an estimated 100-108M for Apple Music. The DMA is the template, and its spread to other jurisdictions is the regulatory risk to monitor.

| Product | Leader | Challenger | Niche | Emerging threat | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone (premium) | Apple | Samsung | Google Pixel | Huawei in China; foldables | S94, S87 |
| Mac | Lenovo by units | Apple | HP and Dell premium tiers | Snapdragon Windows PCs | S95 |
| Wearables | Xiaomi by units, Apple by value | Huawei | Oura in rings, Meta in glasses | AI glasses | S85 |
| Services (apps and advertising) | Alphabet in advertising | Apple in app distribution | Spotify in music | DMA-enabled alternative stores | S15, S93, S77 |

The status quo is a formidable competitor: consumers are holding devices longer, IDC expects China's recovery only in 2028-2029 and forecasts a smaller, more concentrated market after the memory crisis, and the cheapest segment is disappearing [S87, S84, S17, S93]. Pipeline threats are Apple's own foldable in H2 2026, Huawei's HarmonyOS expansion, Google's Gemini-integrated Pixel and AI agents that could move the assistant layer off the operating system. Apple's wedge is the integration of silicon, OS and an installed base that reached an all-time high in Q3 FY2026, which lets it earn 40% product gross margins while rivals earn single digits or lose money; that wedge supports profit-share gains but not unit-share gains. The competitive position therefore supports a quality-compounder view with a regulated ceiling on services, not a share-gain growth story. Confidence is medium-high on hardware and China and medium on services because take rates are in flux. Diligence questions: how much of the premium gain is price inflation, how fast EU developers shift to external distribution, whether Huawei can export HarmonyOS, and whether Apple's foldable holds 40% of the category beyond 2027.

| Quadrant | Points | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strengths | 65% of premium phone units; 40.1% product gross margin; $120.5B services at 76.3% gross margin; installed base at an all-time high; iPhone 50.4% of FY2025 revenue | S94, S17, S6, S5 |
| Weaknesses | 18.1% China share behind Huawei; 15.5% wearables unit share; no advertising scale; revenue concentrated in one product | S87, S85, S5 |
| Opportunities | Foldables above 17M units by 2027 at a $2,550+ ASP; services advertising and cloud; Mac share gains; an AI upgrade cycle | S84, S95 |
| Threats | DMA 5% take rate on external distribution; Huawei premium share; memory costs up more than 300%; AI assistants commoditising the OS layer | S77, S87, S84 |
:::

::: evidence
**Apple's competitive advantage is profit capture, not unit share.**

Apple holds 20% of phone units but 65% of premium units and 36-43% of market value (Counterpoint, S94; IDC, S84). Its 40.1% product gross margin compares with Xiaomi's 8.5% handset margin and a loss at Samsung's mobile division (S17, S90, S91). The vulnerabilities are China and regulation, not pricing power (S87, S77).
:::

Apple's moat is real but uneven: in-house silicon, operating-system control and a very large installed base are hard to replicate, while the intelligence layer the current upgrade cycle is sold on has been rented from Google, so AI protects the franchise without widening it. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, announced on 2026-09-09 and on sale from 2026-09-18, start at $1,199 and $1,299, ship the 2nm A20 Pro and run iOS 27 with a Siri rebuilt on Gemini; iPhone net sales were $54.25bn in the quarter to 2026-06-27, up 22%, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn over nine months as capital spending fell. [S113, S6]

### The hardware cycle is being re-priced, not matured

Apple split its launch: the Pro, Pro Max and the first foldable, iPhone Duo, arrived in September 2026, while the standard iPhone 18, 18e and a second-generation Air are reported for spring 2027, and the iPhone 17 was repriced to $899. The mechanism is deliberate — sell the expensive, 2nm-constrained models into the holiday quarter and the volume models in March, when yields and memory supply have matured. The split turns one spike into two. The risk is elasticity: prices rose into a memory-cost cycle, and the December 2026 quarter is the first test of whether buyers follow. [S112]

### Siri shipped, two years late and in beta

Siri AI went out with iOS 27 on 2026-09-14 as a beta in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish promised for October — roughly 23 months after Apple Intelligence first shipped in October 2024, and after the personalised-Siri promise slipped in 2025. The assistant underneath is a multi-year Google Gemini deal confirmed on 2026-01-12, reported by Bloomberg at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and about $1bn a year; neither company confirmed the price. Apple's own contribution is the interface, personal context, onscreen awareness, camera input and Private Cloud Compute. Apple bought the part of the stack it could not ship in time. [S111, S122]

::: evidence
**The flagship AI feature runs on a competitor's frontier model and a competitor's chips.** Google confirmed a multi-year deal on 2026-01-12 to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at roughly $1bn a year and 1.2 trillion parameters, while Apple's own foundation models were trained on 8,192 Google TPU v4 and 2,048 TPU v5p chips rented through Google Cloud. Apple keeps the interface, the data boundary and the device; it does not keep the model or the compute. [S111, S118]
:::

### The AI bill lands in R&D, not capex

R&D of $34.04bn in nine months, up from $25.68bn, is attributed to AI infrastructure and headcount, while payments for property, plant and equipment fell to $6.80bn from $9.47bn. Free cash flow stays intact, the buyback continues, and the company avoids building datacentres whose utilisation it cannot control. The cost is that the marginal AI dollar is an operating expense with no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. A 33% R&D increase with no disclosed AI revenue line is a margin question, not a technology one. [S6]

### Silicon is the layer still widening

| Distribution | Own devices and services | Android, Pixel, search | Devices | China-led | S111 |

### Where the moat actually sits

| Barrier | Difficulty (1-10) | Why | Time to replicate | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Manufacturing process know-how | 6 | AI-matched hinge, confocal scanning, 25 printed micro-layers | 3-4 years | S114 |
| Frontier AI model | 3 | Bought from Google, no frontier training at scale | 1-2 years, by licence | S111, S118 |
| Developer and services ecosystem | 8 | $91.73bn nine-month services revenue, defaults under pressure | 5+ years | S6 |
| **Composite** | **6.5/10** | Hardware barrier real, intelligence barrier rented | 3-4 years on hardware | — |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone 18 Pro / Pro Max | Shipping | 2026-09-18 | iPhone $54.25bn in Q3 FY2026, +22% | Not disclosed by model | December 2026 mix | S113, S6 |
| iPhone Duo (foldable) | Shipping | Announced 2026-09-09 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Durability and returns | S114 |
| Services | Shipping | Ongoing | $91.73bn in nine months, +14% | 76.3% | DMA compliance | S6 |
| Wearables and Vision Pro | Shipping | Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, SE 3 in FY2025 | Not separately disclosed | Not disclosed | Health-feature adoption | S5, S124 |

If Apple used the Gemini term as a bridge to its own model, the dependency is temporary. Until then the technology case rests on silicon, yield and switching costs, and the AI case rests on distribution. Confidence is high on machine facts, medium on model economics, low on patents.

The cost is that the marginal AI dollar has no asset behind it, and bargaining power sits with the supplier that also owns Android. ### Silicon is the layer still widening

The A20 Pro's move to 2nm from the A19's 3nm, and the in-house C2 modem reported across the iPhone 18 line, are the parts of the stack Apple still owns end to end. ### Where the moat actually sits

|---|---|---|---|---|

The replication test favours the hardware story. It is a monthly alert, not a blood-pressure measurement, so the clinical claim is narrow. Vision Pro remains inside the Wearables line with no disclosed revenue and no confirmed successor. These deepen the installed base and add upgrade reasons; they are sold as features, not as platforms with their own economics.

funding_valuation.author: Valuation Analyst
funding_valuation.markdown:
Apple is an exceptional franchise priced as a perpetual compounder. At $344.63 on NasdaqGS in US dollars (20:00 UTC, 2026-10-30) the equity is capitalised at $5,029.6bn and the enterprise at $4,967.4bn, which is 39.5x trailing earnings and 38.8x trailing NOPAT of $128.1bn. Those multiples need either 6.4-6.9% growth in perpetuity at a 9.0-9.5% discount rate, or a 7.0% discount rate on the growth I forecast below. Both are demanding for a company whose revenue compounded at 5.0% a year from FY2021 [S7, S6, S97].

| Metric | Value | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $344.63, 2026-10-30 20:00 UTC, NasdaqGS, USD | 2% below the 52-week high | S7 |
| Market cap / enterprise value | $5,029.6bn / $4,967.4bn | Largest in the peer set | S7 |
| 52-week range | $243.42-$351.73; price at the 93rd percentile | Uptrend intact | S7 |
| Returns | 1M +3.5%, 3M +11.6%, 12M +27.5%; vs S&P 500 +4.4, +10.4, +16.6 points; vs XLK +11.8, +9.2, +8.1 points | Leadership, and a haven inside a falling tech sector | S7, S12 |
| Moving averages | 50-day $333.04 (+3.5%); 200-day $296.56 (+16.2%) | Above both | S7 |
| Liquidity | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn a day (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | Any plausible position | S7 |
| Cash returned | Dividend 0.31% plus buyback 1.6% = 1.9% | Thin for a 39.5x stock | S6 |
| Multiples | 39.5x P/E trailing, 35.2x forward, 10.6x EV/Sales, 32.1x EV/EBIT | Top of the five-year range | S7, S97 |
| Consensus revenue | iPhone $252.4bn FY2026 and $277.4bn FY2027 | 9.9% growth priced for FY2027 | S71 |

On forward earnings the shares are less stretched than the trailing figure suggests: 35.2x sits almost exactly on the twelve-month average of 35.7x, and earnings are growing. What has changed is the premium to everyone else. Apple pays 39.5x trailing earnings against a peer median of 20.2x and 32.1x EV/EBIT against 20.5x, a 57% premium that only Microsoft at 23.6x comes near; Alphabet, growing faster over the last year, trades at 14.6x. The premium is earned on margin and returns — 48.7% gross margin and 148.8% return on equity, both without peer in the group — not on growth, which is why it is a premium that the discount rate, rather than the operating story, controls [S7, S97, S14].

| Company | P/E (TTM) | EV/EBIT | EV/Sales | FCF yield | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple | 39.5x | 32.1x | 10.6x | 2.7% | S7 |
| Microsoft | 27.3x | 23.6x | 11.1x | 1.5% | S14 |
| Alphabet | 14.6x | 21.2x | 7.1x | 0.6% | S15 |
| Meta | 21.0x | 19.9x | 6.6x | 1.8% | S110 |
| Amazon | 19.4x | 25.5x | 3.3x | n/m | S108 |
| Dell | 24.7x | 21.0x | 2.0x | 3.1% | S106 |
| HP | 11.0x | 9.6x | 0.5x | 15.0% | S104 |
| Peer median | 20.2x | 20.5x | 2.7x | 2.5% | — |

Samsung Electronics and Xiaomi file no US GAAP statements and no market multiple for either was retrieved in this run, so their comparison is not disclosed; the hardware leg leans on HP and Dell.

The operating story that supports 39.5x is real but narrower than the headline. The June 2026 quarter grew revenue 16.4% to $109.4bn, with iPhone up 21.7% and Greater China up 22.4%, and management guided the September quarter to 9-11% growth with iPhone in the mid-teens. Against that, IDC expects global smartphone shipments to fall 16.7% in 2026, and TrendForce puts the iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials up 38% year on year with memory at 34% of it, from about 10% a year earlier. Apple is growing by price, mix and share capture in a shrinking unit market while its hardware cost base rises; Samsung's mobile division lost money in the same quarter for the same reason. Price-led growth is the most reversible kind, and FY2027 gross margin, not revenue, is where the memory cycle will show [S17, S84, S99, S72].

Free cash flow is the number the buyback and the model rest on, and the trailing figure flatters. Trailing FCF of $136.7bn is a 2.7% yield, but nine-month operating cash flow rose $35.2bn year on year of which $25.2bn came from a swing in other current and non-current liabilities (+$10.0bn against -$15.2bn), not from profit. Normalising that swing leaves about $111.5bn, a 2.2% FCF yield and 45x P/FCF. Capital expenditure is rising from a low base at 0.77x depreciation, and research and development grew 32.5% to $34.0bn in the nine months, which caps the margin expansion the multiple assumes [S6].

A discounted cash flow is the right instrument for a company whose value is almost all terminal, and the least forgiving. I take FY2026 revenue of $477.0bn (nine months actual of $364.4bn plus the guided $112.7bn fourth quarter), growth fading from 9% to 5%, a 33% operating margin, a 17.5% tax rate and capital expenditure 0.2 points above depreciation. At a 9.0% cost of equity — a 4.93% ten-year Treasury, a 4.5% equity risk premium and a 1.05 beta — the shares are worth $212. The grid shows why the answer is contested: the market price is reached only near a 7.0% discount rate, and each 50bp on the rate moves value by 15-18%. That is the whole question, whether a 4.93% risk-free rate leaves room for a 7% required return on equity [S10, S6, S72].

|---|---|---|---|
| DCF | WACC 9.0%, terminal growth 4.0%, revenue 9/8/7/6/5%, margin 33%, tax 17.5% | $212 | S6, S10, S72 |
| DCF, discount rate 8.5% / 9.5% | as above | $229 / $193 | S6, S10 |
| DCF, discount rate 7.0% | as above | $352 | S6, S10 |
| Sum of the parts | 23x services EBIT of $62.7bn, 12x hardware EBIT of $92.1bn, plus $62.2bn net cash | $177 | S6, S17, S14, S104 |
| Sum of the parts, upper | 28x services, 18x hardware | $238 | S6, S17 |
| Own-history multiple | 31.0x four-year mean P/E on implied FY2027 EPS of $9.79 | $303 | S7, S97 |
| Market | $344.63 | implies a 7.0% discount rate | S7 |

| WACC / terminal growth | 3.0% | 4.0% | 5.0% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.5% | $244 | $302 | $408 |
| 8.5% | $193 | $229 | $285 |
| 9.5% | $168 | $193 | $228 |

All cells: my DCF on the base operating case (revenue growth 9/8/7/6/5%, 33% operating margin, 17.5% tax), FY2026 revenue $477.0bn [S6, S10, S72].

| Scenario | Revenue growth FY2027-31 | Margin, discount rate | Value per share | vs $344.63 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull: AI cycle plus foldable | 14/11/9/7/6% | 35%, 8.5% | $277 | -20% | My DCF |
| Base | 9/8/7/6/5% | 33%, 9.0% | $212 | -38% | My DCF |
| Bear: memory costs, services remedy | 4/3/2/2/2% | 30%, 9.5% | $133 | -61% | My DCF |
| Market multiple cross-check | 27x / 31x / 35x FY2027 EPS of $9.79 | — | $264 / $303 / $343 | -23% / -12% / 0% | S7, S97 |

Splitting Apple up shows how much of the price is a single-security premium. Services produced $120.5bn of trailing revenue at a 76.0% gross margin and hardware $346.3bn at 39.1%; allocating the $72.3bn of operating expense 40/60 toward services gives services EBIT of about $62.7bn and hardware of $92.1bn. At 23x and 12x — between Microsoft's 23.6x and HP's 9.6x — the parts plus $62.2bn of net cash are worth $177 a share, or $238 at 28x and 18x. The gap to $344.63 is what investors pay for one liquid compounder with a fortress balance sheet. The largest single risk inside services is the Google default-search payment, estimated at about $20bn a year; the remedies ruling in United States v. Google barred exclusivity without banning the payments, which reduces that risk to a renegotiation rather than a loss, though the case is on appeal [S5, S70, S101].

Three scenarios bracket the answer. Even the bull case, with revenue growing 14% next year and margins at 35%, is worth $277 — 20% below the market; the bear case is $133, and a simple re-rating to 27x forward earnings is $264. Buying at $344.63 means buying the multiple rather than the business. A 9% three-year return needs an entry near $270, as the exit analysis sets out, or evidence that EPS grows above 12% rather than the 9.9% that consensus prices for iPhone in FY2027 [S71, S7].

The counter-case deserves its weight. Apple grew earnings per share by more than a quarter in the June quarter, the shares have beaten the S&P 500 by a double-digit margin over twelve months, and the discount rate in my model is a judgement, not an observation: at the low end of the plausible range the base case comes close to the market price. Quality franchises in a high-rate world have held premium multiples for years, and a valuation-led bear case has been premature for two years, as the twelve-month return in the trading table shows. What I will not concede is that the price offers a margin of safety: on every operating assumption I can defend, the buyer's return is set by the exit multiple, and that multiple already sits at the top of its five-year range. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and medium on the gap to intrinsic value, because it rests on a cost of equity nobody observes. The open gap is consensus revenue, EPS and FCF for FY2027-28 and a sell-side price target, none of which any source in this run disclosed.

strategy.author: Product Analyst
strategy.markdown:
Apple's strategy is to keep platform control and cash returns while buying the AI capability it did not build, which works financially but leaves the next upgrade cycle dependent on hardware mix, services growth and a competitor's model. In the first nine months of FY2026 Apple spent $34.04bn on research and development (+33%), $6.80bn on property, plant and equipment (down from $9.47bn) and $62.1bn buying back its own shares, while services grew 14% to $91.73bn at a 76.3% gross margin. The allocation is unambiguous: the balance sheet funds shareholders, the income statement funds AI. [S6]

### Capital returns come before capital projects

FY2025 set the pattern — $89.3bn of buybacks, $15.4bn of dividends, a new $100bn authorisation announced in May 2025 and a quarterly dividend raised to $0.26, against $34.55bn of R&D, up 10%. R&D is now growing three times faster than that, yet none of the increase goes into owned infrastructure. Returning cash while renting intelligence keeps return on equity high and removes the risk of stranded datacentres, but it also means Apple has no AI asset that a competitor cannot rent on similar terms. If features fail to lift average selling price, the R&D step-up is a pure margin cost, and the buyback is what keeps earnings per share intact. The investor gets a capital-return story with an AI expense line, not an AI investment cycle.

### Tariff insurance is being bought with margin

Apple assembled 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, up from 36 million, taking India to 25% of the 220-230 million made globally; Foxconn, Tata Electronics and Pegatron now build every iPhone 17 model there, including the Pro and Pro Max. The strategy is insurance against tariffs and China concentration, and it is working on volume. It is not free: assembly and components still cost more in India than in China or Vietnam, and smartphone production subsidies expired on 2026-03-31, with Apple and peers lobbying New Delhi for a further round. India is also becoming a demand market — sales above $9bn, six stores and Apple Pay planned for 2026. The hedge is real; the margin benefit is not yet. [S115]

### Services funds the strategy; regulation taxes it

Services is the profit engine, and its growth is concentrated where regulation bites: advertising and cloud services drove the 14% increase in the nine months to 2026-03-28 and 2026-06-27, at a gross margin roughly 1.5 times the company average. The Digital Markets Act makes that position contestable. By 2026-03-22 Apple had received 56 interoperability requests under Article 6(7), closing 43 of them and keeping 27 closures fully confidential, while continuing to challenge the obligations. Each request is engineering time and a potential loss of default status, which is the mechanism by which services margins are defended. Apple's response has been to comply narrowly and litigate broadly. [S6, S119]

### The AI layer is a partnership, not a programme

The defining strategic choice of the cycle was made on 2026-01-12, when Google confirmed a multi-year deal to supply Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, reported at a 1.2-trillion-parameter model and $1bn a year. Apple paired that with rented Google TPU capacity for its own foundation models rather than building training clusters. The logic is defensible: ship a competitive assistant on time, keep the interface, the personal context and the Private Cloud Compute boundary, and let a rival absorb the cost of frontier training. The price is strategic: the supplier also owns Android and can price the licence at renewal, and Apple's own research output, while still credible, now sits behind a rented frontier. Platform control is preserved at the layer users see; it is ceded at the layer that determines capability.

| Partner | Scope | Signed or dated | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google (Alphabet) | Gemini models for the rebuilt Siri, multi-year | 2026-01-12 | Confirmed by Google | S111 |
| Google Cloud | TPU training capacity for Apple foundation models | 2024, disclosed in Apple's model paper | In use | S118 |
| Foxconn, Tata Electronics, Pegatron | India assembly of the full iPhone line | Ongoing; 55 million units in 2025 | Operating | S115 |
| Klarna | Apple Upgrade device leasing in the U.S. | 2026, with iPhone 18 | Launched | S113 |

### The talent question is the weak link

The partnership was necessary partly because the in-house programme lost people: through 2025 Apple's AI executives and researchers left, mostly for Meta, which paid to recruit them. Headcount-related expense is one of the two drivers Apple cites for the R&D increase, so the company is paying more for a team that is smaller at the top than it was two years ago. Apple still publishes competitive inference research, which argues against the strongest version of the decline story, but a research organisation that is rebuilt while its flagship assistant runs on a licensed model is a programme in transition, not a moat under construction. [S121]

### Second curves: health and foldables are adjacencies; Vision is not yet one

Health is the most defensible adjacency because it is regulated and sticky: hypertension notifications on Apple Watch carry FDA clearance and peer-reviewed scrutiny, and they give owners a reason to upgrade and a reason not to leave. The foldable Duo is the other extension, priced above the Pro Max and manufactured with a hinge that depends on AI-matched assembly and 3D printing rather than on scale alone. Vision Pro has no disclosed revenue, sits inside the Wearables line and has no confirmed successor, which makes it a research option rather than a growth curve. The test of an adjacency is whether it earns its capital; health and foldables plausibly do, and the headset does not yet.

### What the next twelve months must prove

exit.author: Valuation Analyst
exit.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and net buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to about 1% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below roughly $270, where the three-year return spans 5-13% around a 10% central case, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

| Metric | Value | Implication | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average daily volume | 40.41m shares and $13.84bn (20-day); 41.34m and $13.56bn (3-month) | A $250m position is 1.8% of one day's value traded; $1bn is 7.2% | S7 |
| Shares outstanding | 14,697,926,000 at 2026-01-02 | Free float effectively 100% | S11 |
| Largest holders | Vanguard 9.63%; BlackRock 7.10% | Index managers, no controlling or strategic holder | S11 |
| Directors and officers | 9,079,765 shares, 0.06% | Aligned, but immaterial to the register | S11 |
| Index role | Largest in the peer set; the weight itself is not publicly disclosed in the sources here | A structural passive bid, and a source of correlated selling in redemptions | S7 |

Liquidity is the one exit risk that can be dismissed. Apple trades $13.8bn a day, so a position of any size a long-only fund would take can be liquidated inside a week at a market impact measured in single-digit basis points, and the exit is never closed. What cannot be dismissed is price: the buyers on the other side are the same index and active funds the seller competes with, and in a broad de-rating they all mark the same multiple down together [S7].

| Component | Rate | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Dividend yield | 0.31% ($1.08 annualised on $344.63) | S17, S7 |
| Buyback yield, gross | 1.63% ($82.2bn repurchased on a $5,029.6bn market value) | S6, S7 |
| Buyback yield, net of $13.7bn stock compensation | 1.36% | S6, S7 |
| Total shareholder yield | 1.94% | S6, S7 |
| EPS growth, FY2021 to TTM / FY2026E to FY2029E | 9.2% / 8.0% | S1, S6 |
| Of the historic growth, from a falling share count | 2.7 points a year | S1, S6 |
| Three-year return, multiple unchanged | 9.9% a year | S7, S97 |
| Three-year return, multiple reverts to 31.0x | 1.3% a year | S7, S97 |

Two things follow. First, the operating return is real but modest: a 1.9% yield plus 8% earnings growth is a high-single-digit compounding machine, not the 27.5% twelve-month return the shares have just delivered. Second, the buyback does most of the work in that growth, and at 39.5x it buys a 2.5% earnings yield per dollar spent — below the 4.93% ten-year Treasury — so the repurchase supports the share price without creating value at this level. The mechanism is not a scandal; it is what a mature cash machine should do with cash it cannot reinvest at its own cost of capital. But an investor paying 39.5x is paying for the cash return, not receiving a bargain from it [S6, S1].

The multiple, not the business, is the swing factor. Apple traded at 24.6x at the end of FY2022, 27.9x in FY2023, 37.5x in FY2024 and 34.2x in FY2025; it now trades at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward, against a twelve-month average of 35.7x. A reversion to the four-year mean of 31.0x costs 21.5% of the price, or 7.7% a year over three years, which swallows the entire shareholder yield and most of the earnings growth. That is the mechanism the higher-rate regime exerts on a long-duration equity: with the ten-year Treasury at 4.93%, up 84 basis points in a year, the discount applied to cash flows arriving after 2035 is materially higher than it was when the shares traded at 27.9x [S7, S97, S10].

| Route | Named buyer or venue | Rationale | Timing | Likelihood | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

exit.author: Valuation Analyst
exit.markdown:
Apple's exit is the public market and its own buyback, not a buyer. No company in the peer set is large enough to acquire it — Microsoft at $3,875.8bn, Alphabet at $3,461.1bn, Amazon at $2,598.9bn and Meta at $1,582.4bn are all smaller than Apple's $5,029.6bn market value — so a holder's realisation depends entirely on the multiple another investor will pay. With dividend and gross buyback yielding 1.9% and earnings per share compounding at 8-9%, the arithmetic is adequate only while the 39.5x multiple holds; if it reverts toward the four-year average of 31.0x, the three-year return from $344.63 falls to 1.3% a year. That sets the sell discipline: buy below $270, where the three-year return spans 5.0-13.3% around 9.9%, and treat $380 and above as a sale [S7, S11, S6].

company_overview.author: Company Analyst
company_overview.markdown:
Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality.

### What a buyer actually owns

Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. [S11]

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Share classes and votes | 1 class, 1 vote; 50.4bn authorised; 14.70bn outstanding | Alphabet issues Class C alongside voting shares | good | S5, S11, S125 |
| Free float | 99.94% (insiders 9,079,765 shares) | No strategic or state holder | good | S11 |
| Board independence | 7 of 8 directors; 7 of 9 from 2026-09-01 | Majority independent | warn | S11, S56 |
| Independent director tenure | 12.0-year average; longest 26 years | Apple's age-75 re-election guideline | warn | S11 |
| Capital returned vs free cash flow | $106.1bn vs $98.8bn (107%), FY2025 | 100% of free cash flow | warn | S5 |
| Effective tax rate | 15.6% FY2025 vs 24.1% FY2024 | Prior year | warn | S5 |
| iPhone share of revenue | 53.9% in 9M FY2026 vs 51.2% in 9M FY2025 | Prior year | warn | S17 |
:::

### The entity map is simple; the profit map was not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Inc. | California, US | Corporation (registrant) | Group parent; designs, sells, holds IP | 100% of group | No controlling holder | S5, S11 |
| Apple Operations International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US holding and operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Distribution International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US distribution | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Asia Ltd | Hong Kong | Limited company | Regional sales and procurement | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, US | Corporation | Treasury vehicle; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Insurance Company, Inc. | Arizona, US | Corporation | Captive insurance; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |

Every listed subsidiary is wholly owned; Exhibit 21 omits entities that are not significant in aggregate, so no complete group list is public, and the 10-K does not say which two Irish subsidiaries held the branches at issue. The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. Irish law had already closed the opinions from January 2015. [S5]

Two consequences follow. The tax rate is now policy-driven rather than engineered: 24.1% in FY2024, 15.6% in FY2025, with no filing supporting a return to the pre-2015 structure. And the entity map carries no enforceability premium — the legal risk attached to it is regulatory rather than structural, a materially better position than a contractually controlled China VIE.

### Business model: one platform, one rent, one budget owner

Apple sells integrated hardware to consumers, small businesses, education, enterprise and government, then monetises the installed base through Services. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. The end user is usually the buyer, but the budget owner for the highest-margin line is the developer and the subscriber: Services earned a 75.4% gross margin against 36.8% for products. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. In the nine months to 2026-06-27 iPhone was 53.9% of revenue against 51.2% a year earlier and Services 25.2%, so concentration is rising again rather than falling. [S5, S17]

### Governance: senior, stable, slow to refresh

Eight directors stood in 2026: seven independent plus the CEO. Independent tenure averages 12.0 years — Levinson 26 years and chair since 2000, Jung 18, Sugar 16, Wagner 12, Lozano and Gorsky 5, Austin 2 — and two of the seven (Levinson, 75; Sugar, 77) are at or past the company's own guideline that directors generally may not stand for re-election after 75. Committees are conventional and fully independent: Audit under Sugar (nine meetings in 2025), People and Compensation under Jung, Nominating under Wagner; 92% of votes cast supported say-on-pay in 2025. From 2026-09-01 the structure shifts in a way that matters: Ternus joins as CEO and Cook becomes Executive Chair, taking non-independent directors to two of nine (77.8%) and replacing an independent chair with a lead independent director. [S11, S56]

### A clean structure is not a clean earnings record

The forensic problem is optical, not legal. FY2025 returned $106.1bn — $90.7bn of buybacks and $15.4bn of dividends — against free cash flow of $98.8bn, or 107% of it, while diluted EPS rose 22.7% against an 8.0% rise in operating income and the effective tax rate fell to 15.6% from 24.1%. Diluted shares fell 6.9%, from 15,812,547,000 in FY2023 to 14,714,676,000 in Q3 FY2026, and $263.2bn of buybacks over three years bought the arithmetic. That is how a mature hardware company reports high-teens EPS growth; it is also what stops working the year the buyback slows. Counter-evidence is genuine: Q3 FY2026 revenue grew 16% and gross margin reached 50.1%, so FY2026 is not an optical year. [S5, S17]

### Where the judgement breaks, and what to settle

Three events would change the call: a structural remedy in the DOJ monopolisation suit or the DMA Article 6(4) file that reaches commission economics would compress the 75.4% services margin; a board that keeps the executive-chair arrangement past 2027 would entrench a post-CEO chair; and a buyback slowdown would expose the underlying operating growth rate. Confidence is high on identity, ownership and capital-return facts and medium on the board's appetite for refresh, because its own age guideline is already being waived for two members. Diligence should settle whether that waiver was formal and who chairs the board after 2027; whether BlackRock's stake has moved since 2023; what share of Services revenue depends on US third-party payment rules; and the FY2026 buyback pace under the $100bn authorisation of 2025-05-01. [S11, S5]

::: timeline
| Date | Event | Significance | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1976-04-01 | Founded as a partnership by Jobs, Wozniak and Wayne | Origin; incorporated 1977-01-03 | S126 |
| 1980-12-12 | IPO at $22 per share, over $100m raised | Public listing; single-class equity | S126 |
| 1997-06 | NeXT acquired; Jobs returns as CEO | Reset to an integrated hardware and software model | S126 |
| 2007-06-29 | iPhone launched | Creates the platform and the App Store rent | S126 |
| 2011-08 | Cook becomes CEO, after COO since October 2005 | Operator era; capital-return model begins | S11 |
| 2016-08-30 | Commission orders Ireland to recover state aid | Irish profit allocation becomes a liability | S5 |
| 2024-03-21 | DOJ and state attorneys general file monopolisation suit | Services rent contested in the US | S5 |
| 2024-09-10 | Court of Justice confirms the state aid decision | $10.2bn net charge; $15.8bn paid to Ireland | S5 |
| 2025-04-23 | EUR 500m DMA fine and cease-and-desist order | EU remedy risk on app steering | S5 |
| 2025-05-01 | New $100bn buyback authorised | Capital return continues at scale | S5 |
| 2025-12-01 | Giannandrea steps down; AI moves under Federighi | AI reorganisation | S127 |
| 2026-04-20 | Ternus named CEO from 2026-09-01; Cook Executive Chair; Levinson Lead Independent | First CEO change since 2011 | S56 |
:::

company_overview.author: Company Analyst
company_overview.markdown:
Apple is legally and structurally clean enough to hold for years — one share class, one registrant, no VIE and a genuinely unblocked exit — but its governance has barely refreshed in a decade and two of seven independents sit at Apple's own age-75 ceiling, so the holding should be underwritten on cash generation and clean title rather than on board quality. Apple Inc. is a California corporation incorporated on 1977-01-03, listed on Nasdaq under AAPL in US dollars. At 2026-01-02 it had 14,697,926,000 shares outstanding against 50,400,000,000 authorised, all of a single class of $0.00001 par common stock with one vote per share. There is no dual-class structure, no VIE, no nominee shareholder and no contractual control chain — verified in the balance sheet and the 2026 proxy, not assumed. Float is effectively the whole company: directors and officers hold 9,079,765 shares, or 0.06%, leaving 99.94%. Vanguard (9.63%) and BlackRock (7.10%) are the only disclosed 5% holders — and BlackRock's figure rests on a Schedule 13G/A reflecting holdings at 2023-12-31, so the 2026 register is partly unknown. [S11]

::: kpi
| Metric | Value | Benchmark | Signal | Source |

| Free float | 99.94% (insiders 9,079,765 shares) | No strategic or state holder | good | S11 |
| Board independence | 7 of 8 directors; 7 of 9 from 2026-09-01 | Majority independent | warn | S11, S56 |
| Independent director tenure | 12.0-year average; longest 26 years | Apple's age-75 re-election guideline | warn | S11 |

| iPhone share of revenue | 53.9% in 9M FY2026 vs 51.2% in 9M FY2025 | Prior year | warn | S17 |
:::

### The entity map is simple; the profit map was not

| Entity | Jurisdiction | Type | Role | Ownership | Controller | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple Inc. | California, US | Corporation (registrant) | Group parent; designs, sells, holds IP | 100% of group | No controlling holder | S5, S11 |
| Apple Operations International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US holding and operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Operations Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Irish operations | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Distribution International Ltd | Ireland | Limited company | Non-US distribution | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Asia Ltd | Hong Kong | Limited company | Regional sales and procurement | 100% indirect | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Braeburn Capital, Inc. | Nevada, US | Corporation | Treasury vehicle; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |
| Apple Insurance Company, Inc. | Arizona, US | Corporation | Captive insurance; function not disclosed | 100% | Apple Inc. | S5 |

Every listed subsidiary is wholly owned; Exhibit 21 omits entities that are not significant in aggregate, so no complete group list is public, and the 10-K does not say which two Irish subsidiaries held the branches at issue. The structure that mattered economically was profit allocation, not ownership: Irish branches operated under tax opinions issued in 1991 and 2007, which the Commission treated as state aid on 2016-08-30. The General Court annulled that decision on 2020-07-15, the Court of Justice set the annulment aside on 2024-09-10, and Apple booked a one-time $10.2bn net charge in Q4 FY2024 — $15.8bn payable to Ireland from escrow, offset by a $4.8bn US foreign tax credit. FY2025 net sales were $416,161m, split $307,003m products and $109,158m services, with 40% direct and 60% indirect distribution. Growth comes from installed-base expansion and price/mix, not unit share — Apple states it holds a minority share of global smartphones, PCs, tablets and wearables. team.author: Company Analyst
team.markdown:
The team is deep in the functions that built the iPhone era — hardware, operations, finance — and thin where the next era is being decided: AI accountability was reorganised in December 2025 into Craig Federighi's software organisation after the Siri delay, the chip chief was reported to be considering leaving, and the new CEO is a hardware engineer who has never run a services or regulatory fight, so the platform is being defended by continuity rather than by a bench built for the transition. Apple is run by career insiders — Cook has been at the company since March 1998 (28 years), Ternus since 2001 (25 years), and the 2025 CFO and COO appointments were internal promotions. Ternus's hardware organisation and the silicon team invent; Cook built worldwide sales before 2005 and O'Brien runs retail; Cue's organisation holds the App Store rent; Parekh allocates the capital, $106.1bn returned in FY2025; Federighi's software organisation took over AI on 2025-12-01. [S11, S56]

| Executive | Degree | Institution | Year | Focus | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tim Cook, CEO 2011-2026, Executive Chair from 2026-09-01 | Not disclosed in proxy or 10-K | — | — | — | S11, S56 |
| John Ternus, CEO from 2026-09-01 | B.S. Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics; minor in psychology | University of Pennsylvania | 1997 | Mechanical engineering | S130 |
| Kevan Parekh, CFO from 2025-01-01 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Sabih Khan, COO from 2025 | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Deirdre O'Brien, SVP Retail + People | Not disclosed in proxy | — | — | — | S11 |
| Jennifer Newstead, SVP, General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S132 |
| Amar Subramanya, VP of AI from 2025-12 | Not disclosed in Apple filings | — | — | — | S127 |

Apple's proxy is unusual among mega-caps in disclosing no degrees for any named executive; only Ternus's 1997 Penn engineering degree is established from a university record. The gap is material because the CEO's technical formation is the main public evidence of whether he can referee a models-and-silicon roadmap.

| Period | Executive | Role | Evidence of scope | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1998-03 to 2000-10 | Tim Cook | SVP, Worldwide Operations | Supply and operations remit | S11 |
| 2002-02 to 2005-10 | Tim Cook | EVP, Worldwide Sales and Operations | Sales added to operations | S11 |
| 2005-10 to 2011-08 | Tim Cook | Chief Operating Officer | Ran the company through product cycles | S11 |
| 2011-08 to 2026-09-01 | Tim Cook | CEO | Cumulative TSR +2,162% and market capitalisation +$3.4trn, 2011-2025 | S11 |
| 2001 to 2013 | John Ternus | Product design team, then VP Hardware Engineering from 2013 | Product development | S56, S130 |
| 2021 to 2026-09-01 | John Ternus | SVP, Hardware Engineering | Largest product organisation | S56 |
| 2025-01-01 to present | Kevan Parekh | SVP, CFO | Previously VP, Financial Planning and Analysis | S11 |
| 2025 to present | Sabih Khan | SVP, COO | On the executive team since 2019, previously SVP Operations | S11 |
| 2017 to 2026-03 | Kate Adams | SVP, General Counsel and Secretary | Moved to government affairs until retirement in late 2026 | S128, S132 |
| 2026-01 to present | Jennifer Newstead | SVP; General Counsel from 2026-03-01 | External hire, reports to the CEO | S132 |

Pay is where the team is most unusual. Cook's 2025 total target compensation was $59m — a $3m salary unchanged since 2016, a $6m target cash award and a $50m equity award, 75% performance-based — against Satya Nadella's $96.5m reported for Microsoft's fiscal 2025 and Sundar Pichai's $10.9m reported for 2025, though Pichai's 2026 target equity award is $210m and a 1,348,607-share 2022 award vested to him in February 2026. Apple's other named executives each target about $23m: $1m salary, a 200% cash target and $20m of equity. There are no employment contracts, no change-of-control payments and time-based RSUs vest over roughly four and a half years, so retention runs through unvested stock rather than contractual protection — cheap for shareholders and defensible at 92% say-on-pay, but exposed where pay is not disclosed at all. [S11, S129, S125]

::: evidence
**The AI organisation has been rebuilt around software, but no filing names an owner of the AI P&L.**
On 2025-12-01 Apple announced that John Giannandrea, SVP Machine Learning and AI Strategy, was stepping down to advise before retiring in spring 2026; Amar Subramanya joined as VP of AI reporting to Craig Federighi, taking Apple Foundation Models, ML research and AI safety, while the rest of the organisation moved to Sabih Khan and Eddy Cue [S127]. Seven months later the July 2026 results release had Cook announcing "the all-new Siri AI" at WWDC26 [S17] — delivery, but through a structure in which model, product and commercial accountability sit with three different executives.
:::

The reporting on silicon is the sharpest counter-evidence to a continuity story. In December 2025 Johny Srouji, SVP Hardware Technologies and the architect of Apple silicon, was reported to have told Cook he was seriously considering leaving; no departure or new role has been disclosed since. Custom silicon is the mechanism behind both product differentiation and the 36.8% products gross margin, so the loss of its architect would threaten a roadmap competitors cannot copy quickly. Promoting a hardware engineer to CEO may be the retention move that keeps that bench together — or it may not, and the filings will not say which. [S131, S5]

The 2024-26 turnover cluster is the part a reference check should attack. Within about eighteen months Apple changed CFO (2025-01-01), COO (2025), general counsel (2026-03-01, with Adams retained for government affairs until late 2026), AI leadership (2025-12-01), environment leadership (announced 2025-12-04) and CEO (2026-09-01). Apple calls each a planned transition and two successors were internal, which is real bench evidence; but keeping the outgoing general counsel on government affairs signals how heavy the regulatory load has become, and it also means the person who ran the DOJ and DMA fights is leaving while those cases are live. [S11, S128, S132]

| Dimension | Cook | Ternus | Parekh | Khan | Team |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Years at Apple | 28 | 25 | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Deep insider bench |
| Technical depth | Operations and supply chain | Hardware engineering | Finance and FP&A | Operations | Strong on hardware and cost |
| Scaling record | CEO through 15 years and $3.4trn of value added | Largest product organisation | CFO through a 16% growth year | COO across the supply chain | Proven at scale |
| Capital markets | $263.2bn of buybacks in three years | Not evidenced | CFO since 2025 | Not evidenced | Adequate |
| Regulatory and policy | Testified through antitrust era | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Not evidenced | Thin |
| Prior exits or founder roles | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | None disclosed | No founder experience |
| Key-person dependency | High as Executive Chair | High as new CEO | Medium | Medium | High |
| Retention risk | Low; retirement provisions in place | Low; first-year CEO | Medium | Medium | Medium-high |

What public records confirm is narrow and clean: titles, dates, pay, the $59m target, the 2,162% cumulative TSR under Cook and the 92% say-on-pay. What they contradict or cannot settle is larger — no degrees for six of seven executives, no pay or ownership for Federighi, Cue, Srouji or Joswiak because they are not Section 16 filers, no disclosed outcome to the Srouji report, and no named AI owner. For a people-dependent thesis that is a real information discount. Diligence should verify Ternus's non-hardware operating scope and any retention award, the Srouji title and succession, the 2026 awards to non-NEO SVPs, and who signs off the AI roadmap and budget. The company's leadership biographies, which would settle degrees and prior employers, could not be retrieved in this run, so those cells stay "not disclosed" rather than inferred. [S41, S11]

risk.author: Red Team Analyst
risk.markdown:
Apple is a high-quality compounder whose price already capitalises a peak margin and a contested services annuity, so the risks that matter destroy the multiple rather than the balance sheet, and none of them is yet priced at $344.63. At that price on 2026-10-30 the shares trade at 39.5x trailing and 35.2x forward earnings against a 20.2x peer median, and the base DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212. [S7, S97, S10] Nine risks are ranked below: two are fatal to the current price, the rest are execution risks a fund can own through at the right entry. Memory prints quarterly; the D.C. Circuit ruling is binary.

::: risk-matrix
| Risk | Probability | Impact | Level | Timing | Signpost | Mitigation | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Memory cost pushes hardware gross margin below 46% | High, over 60% | EPS -6% per 200bp; -25% to -30% of value | Critical | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | Product margin under 37%; DRAM and NAND prices | Enter at $270; wait for the trough | S17, S6, S99, S136 |
| Google search payment cut or banned on appeal | Medium, 20-25% | EPS -10% to -13%; value -15% to -20% | High | 2027, D.C. Circuit No. 26-5023 | Argument schedule; renewal terms | Cap the position | S70, S76, S135 |
| Multiple reverts to the 31.0x four-year mean | Medium-high, 40-60% | -21.5% at 31x; -38% at 24.6x | High | 0-12 months | Ten-year yield over 5%; forward P/E over 40x | No position at $344.63 | S97, S10 |
| EU DMA fee band spreads to other markets | Medium, 20-40% | EU operating income -1% to -2%; -5% if it spreads | Medium | From 2026-10-01 | Services growth below 10%; developer migration | Underwrite 10-12% services growth | S77, S78, S102 |
| AI cycle fails; Gemini reprices per device | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -5% to -8% | High | FY2027 | Siri beta exit; services margin step-down | Treat AI as a cost line | S111, S6, S137 |
| China demand falls 20% in H2 2026 | Medium, 30-50% | Revenue -3.5%; EPS -5% to -6% | Medium | Q4 FY2026-FY2027 | China revenue; Q4 tracker data | Do not capitalise 30% China growth | S96, S84, S87 |
| Tariffs and supply-chain shock | Medium, 20-40% | EPS -3% to -5% at a 10-point product hit | Medium | Ongoing | New Section 301 lists; India incentive renewal | India at 25% of assembly | S115, S6, S17 |
| Earnings quality: liabilities, intangibles, inventory | Medium, 30-50% | EPS -2% on a 30% inventory write-down | Medium | 10-K, 2026-11-02 | FCF conversion below 0.9x | Use normalised free cash flow | S6, S5 |
| Governance and key-person | Low, under 20% | Value -5% to -10% | Low | 12-24 months | Director retirements; Srouji title | Board refresh; retention | S134, S133, S11 |
:::

### The risk that breaks the thesis is the hardware margin, not the platform

The record 50.1% gross margin carried 2 percentage points of tariff refunds and $0.11 of the $2.02 EPS. Memory prices rose 146% in the first quarter of 2026 against the 2025 average; TrendForce's 30 September 2026 forecast puts conventional DRAM contract prices 10-15% higher quarter on quarter in the fourth quarter and NAND 15-20% higher. The iPhone 18 Pro's bill of materials is up 38% year on year, memory at 34% of it against 10%. Two hundred basis points off the gross margin is $0.52 of EPS, 6.0% of the trailing $8.72; a 46% margin instead of the base case's 47-48% takes FY2027 EPS from $9.79 to roughly $9.3 and, at 29x, puts fair value at $270 — the entry price, not a discount to it. Inventory of $11.1bn against $5.7bn at FY2025 year-end is the write-down channel if higher prices meet elastic demand. [S17, S6, S99, S136]

::: info danger
**A memory-led gross margin below 46% breaks earnings and the multiple at once.** The margin applies to all $466.8bn of revenue, Apple cannot re-price handsets inside a quarter, and 39.5x leaves no room for a 6% EPS cut: 200bp also invites a de-rating from 35x forward to the 31x mean, together a 25-30% drawdown. The signpost is the December-quarter margin guide on 2026-11-02 (S17, S6, S136).
:::

### The search payment is a renegotiation risk until the appeal says otherwise

The US v. Google trial record put Apple's search revenue share at $20bn in 2022 — 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and 15% of operating income. Judge Mehta's remedy barred exclusivity but preserved non-exclusive payments, and the American Antitrust Institute's 4 August 2026 amicus brief confirms that reading when it asks the D.C. Circuit to strike the payment mechanism the district court left in place; Google's appeal, No. 26-5023, and the DOJ's cross-appeal keep the tail live into 2027. I price a 20-25% probability of a ban at -10% to -13% of EPS and -15% to -20% of value once the services multiple de-rates; a lower rate is likelier. The EU fee schedule in force from 2026-10-01 — 26% in-app, 20% alternative payment, 15% link-outs, 5% Core Technology Commission — is modest in situ, since Europe is 26.7% of nine-month revenue and each $1bn of commission lost is $0.75bn of gross profit against $154.9bn of operating income, but material as a template: a 5-15% band extended to the United States would reset services growth to high single digits. [S70, S76, S77, S79, S135]

### AI is a cost line before it is a moat

Siri shipped as an English beta on 2026-09-14, 23 months after Apple Intelligence, on a Gemini model licensed at a reported $1bn a year, while R&D rose 33% to $34.04bn and capital spending fell to $6.80bn. Apple rents the capability and books the bill in operating expense, and no filing names an AI profit-and-loss owner after the 2025-12-01 reorganisation; X Corp. and xAI's suit against Apple and OpenAI survived dismissal, and the same default-placement theory would apply to a Gemini default. A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case is safe while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin. The swing factor is not capability but whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at a $1,199 starting price. [S111, S6, S127, S137]

### China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war

Q3 2026 China shipments fell 10% year on year on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%; Apple gained 4.8 points of share and the iPhone 18 Pro launch sold 23.5% more than its predecessor. The risk is arithmetic: Greater China was 15.5% of FY2025 revenue and 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue, and IDC expects the decline to widen to 20% in the second half of 2026 after a first half that pulled purchases forward; a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs still exceed China's, and Section 301 duties have replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x trailing, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and the multiple is the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough costs 38%, and the realistic drawdown is the $242 on which two independent methods converge. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%, so a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied required return is the whole debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $95.7bn, or 52x, and no longer covers the $82.2bn buyback; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors, not thesis risks. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood for re-election in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO — a refreshment calendar, not a control problem. The December 2025 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer in April 2026 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency. The FY2025 payout that looks stretched is a tax artefact, not cash the company cannot spare. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption that would stop 2nm A20 Pro supply, an appellate remedy that treats the Gemini default as the next search payment, and the liability line matching most of the intangibles added in nine months. None changes the recommendation: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if the December quarter confirms the margin trough.

A $1bn licence is 0.6% of operating income, so the base case holds while pricing is annual; per-device pricing across a 2.5bn installed base would land in the 76.3% services margin, and whether a licensed assistant sells handsets at $1,199 is the swing factor. China is a shrinking pool, not a lost share war: Q3 2026 shipments fell 10% on Counterpoint's count and 15.4% on IDC's, with Apple at 19.5% against Huawei's 21.3%, a 4.8-point gain. Greater China was 17.8% of nine-month FY2026 revenue; IDC sees the decline widening to 20% in the second half of 2026, and a 20% China decline is 3.5% of group revenue and 5-6% of EPS. Supply adds a second layer: 25% of iPhones are assembled in India, where production incentives expired on 2026-03-31 and costs exceed China's, and Section 301 duties replaced the IEEPA tariffs struck down on 2026-02-20. [S111, S6, S127, S137, S96, S84, S87, S115]

### Valuation is the risk the recommendation already prices

At 39.5x, Apple sits at a five-year high for a company guiding 9-11% growth, and 40.2x trailing free cash flow of $125.1bn (39.5-41.0x across the $122.6-127.3bn band, on $5,029.6bn) makes the multiple the largest driver of return: reversion to the 31.0x mean costs 21.5%, reversion to the 24.6x FY2022 trough 38%, and the realistic drawdown is $242. Each 50 basis points on the cost of equity moves the DCF by 15-18%; a 4.93% ten-year Treasury against a 7.0% implied return is the debate. The stress tests separate survivable from fatal: revenue 30% lower at the 43% incremental margin takes operating income to $95bn and EPS to $5.4, the $133 DCF bear; free cash flow 30% lower is $85.8-89.1bn on the band, 56.4-58.6x, which covers the $82.2bn trailing buyback but not $97.9bn of buybacks and dividends; the deferred-consideration case at $123.2bn, 40.8x, changes neither; a 30% inventory write-down is $3.3bn, 1.9% of operating income; 100 basis points on $84.3bn of debt is $0.84bn, 0.5%. Apple survives all of them on $62.2bn of net cash and $146.5bn of securities; the equity does not, which is why the answer is $270 and not $344.63. [S10, S97, S6, S5]

### Governance, unknowns and the call

Governance and key-person risk are monitors. The board waived its age guideline for two directors and both stood in 2026; from 2026-09-01 Apple has a nine-person board, two non-independent, with Cook as Executive Chair and Ternus as CEO. The 2025-12-06 report that Srouji was considering leaving is superseded: he was named Chief Hardware Officer on 2026-04-20 with hardware engineering added to his silicon remit, which concentrates rather than removes the dependency, with no disclosed successor or retention award. The 107% payout is a tax artefact: FY2024 carried a $10.2bn State Aid charge and FY2025 paid $15.8bn of Irish tax. Cash quality is a smaller risk than it looked: a $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities against $13,270M of gross intangibles added, with $1,780M of investing "other", reads as deferred consideration, but net of a $4,128M fall in other current liabilities the build is $9,403M, inside the $10,016M other-liabilities line; if the whole purchase is unpaid, free cash flow is $123.2bn, $1.9bn below the $125.1bn central case and inside the $122.6-127.3bn band rather than the $117.3bn or $111.5bn readings. The 10-K on 2026-11-02 must tie the intangibles to the liability. Outside the filings: a Taiwan Strait disruption stopping 2nm supply, and an appellate remedy treating the Gemini default as the next search payment. The downside is a de-rating, not insolvency, so position size carries the risk; open diligence is narrow: the December-quarter margin guide, the 10-K working-capital note, the appellate schedule and the Gemini renewal terms. None changes the call: the price, not the business, is the problem, and the $270 entry holds only if December confirms the margin trough. [S134, S133, S141, S11, S5, S6]

thesis.author: Lead Analyst
thesis.markdown:
Apple is a genuine compounder priced as a perpetual one. The installed base, the silicon roadmap and the services annuity are real, and FY2026 is a strong trading year: revenue rose 16.4% in the June quarter, iPhone revenue rose 22.4% in the nine months to 27 June 2026, and services earned 40.3% of gross profit on 25.8% of revenue. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price: at $344.63 on 30 October 2026 the shares carry a $5,029.6bn market capitalisation, 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward. The decision is not whether Apple is a good business — it is — but whether a long-only fund should own it at a multiple that assumes the next five years go right [S6, S7, S97, S146].

Three valuation methods agree and none reaches the price. A discounted cash flow at a 9.0% cost of equity, built on the 4.93% ten-year Treasury, gives $212 a share; the bull case at an 8.5% discount rate and a 35% operating margin gives $277; the sum of the parts is $177-238; the stock's own four-year average multiple of 31.0 times implies $303 [S6, S10, S97]. To justify $344.63 an investor needs a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth in net operating profit after tax. Those assumptions make the price exactly fair rather than cheap, and the base rate they must beat is modest: revenue compounded 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025.

The sell side sees fair value where this report sees an 18% overvaluation: the median twelve-month target is $338-355, flat to +3% from the close [S142, S144]. Consensus expects iPhone revenue of $252.4bn in FY2026 and $277.4bn in FY2027 and capitalises the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin. The disagreement is specific: that margin included two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned (the iPhone 18 Pro bill of materials is up 38%, memory 34% of it), and our base case underwrites 47-48%. A 46% margin, which a full memory pass-through implies, takes FY2027 EPS to about $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times — the entry price proposed below, not a discount to it. The non-consensus view is not that Apple is worse than people think; it is that the market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at the same time.

Three scenarios weighted 25/50/25 put the probability-weighted value near $292, 15% below the price. Bull ($357, 25%): the AI and foldable cycle extends iPhone growth into FY2027-28, services grows above 15%, gross margin holds 48% and the search payment survives at a lower rate — 35 times FY2027 EPS of $10.20 for a 4% price return, with the upside coming from a multiple that stays elevated rather than from earnings. Base ($284, 50%): growth fades from 9% to 5%, margin normalises to 47-48%, services grows 12-14% and the search payment is renegotiated lower — 29 times $9.79, an 18% decline, with intrinsic value of $212-264. Bear ($241, 25%): memory breaks the hardware margin below 46%, services growth falls under 8% as the DMA and link-out remedies bite, and the payment is cut or banned — 24.6 times $9.79, a 30% drawdown, with the $133 DCF bear as the permanent-loss tail [S6, S7].

Three analogs set the decision rule. Microsoft's 1998 antitrust case ended in 2001 with the break-up rejected and conduct remedies imposed: the asset survived, but the overhang ran for three years and the resolution did not re-rate the stock — the cloud did, a decade later. Nokia held 49.4% of handset share in 2007, peaked near $250bn and sold its handset business for $7.2bn in 2013: a platform leader that loses the next interface loses developers first and volume second. Cisco took until December 2025 to exceed its March 2000 record, 25 years in which the company compounded and the share price did not [S143, S145, S147]. The rule they teach is that at a peak multiple the entry price, not the business, sets the return. Apple is cheaper than Cisco at its peak (39.5 times against 201), owns silicon and a services annuity Nokia never had, and holds $62.2bn of net cash, so the analogy is about duration and multiple, not extinction.

The decision follows: watchlist today, zero position, with a staged entry set by price, not narrative. A first tranche of 0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270 or below, where a 9% three-year return becomes reachable across 27-34 times exits; a second at $245; the position taken to its 5% cap below $225 or on evidence that FY2027 EPS growth is tracking above 12%. The red-team objection stands: $270 is a 5% discount to the $284 base case and sits above the $242 realistic bear, so it is a first price, not a margin of safety, and the three tranches exist to price that. Sell above $380 or above 45 times forward earnings (about $440), or if two consecutive quarters show services growth below 10%, gross margin below 47%, or a services structure that removes the search payment.

scoring.author: Lead Analyst
scoring.markdown:
The composite score is 6.1 out of 10, and the number describes a good company at a poor price rather than a mediocre one. Six dimensions — moat, unit economics, earnings quality, balance sheet, capital allocation and growth — average above 7; two, valuation and regulation, sit at or below 4; the weighted table below shows where the 6.1 comes from. That split is the recommendation: Watchlist with a staged entry, not Buy, because the price already pays for the quality, and not Avoid, because the franchise would still compound through most of the downside scenarios [S6, S7].

Valuation scores 2 of 10 and carries the largest weight, 20%. At $344.63 the shares trade at 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings, against an S&P 500 at 18.09 times forward and a peer median of 20.2 times; the trailing multiple is 10.8% above Apple's own twelve-month average of 35.66 times [S97, S146, S7]. The DCF at a 9.0% cost of equity is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the market price is matched only at a 7.0% discount rate or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth. The sell side's median target of $338-355 offers flat to +3%, so there is no analyst catalyst to close the gap either.

The quality block is where the score earns its keep. Unit economics score 9: services earn a 76.3% gross margin and 40.3% of group gross profit on 25.8% of revenue, working capital runs at -56.8 days, and capex is 2.2% of revenue. Earnings quality scores 7 and the balance sheet 9: normalised free cash flow of $122.6-125.1bn converts at 0.95-0.97 times net income against 0.50 at Microsoft and 0.08 at Alphabet, net cash is $62,173M, and only $12.4bn of debt matures within a year [S6, S17]. The deduction on earnings quality is deliberate: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, and the FY2026 10-K must settle whether the $13,531M rise in other non-current liabilities is an unpaid intangible purchase.

Growth scores 5 and regulation 4, and together they explain why the recommendation is not merely to wait for a cheaper multiple. Revenue compounded 3.3% a year from FY2021 to FY2025 and 5.0% to the last twelve months; the 2026 acceleration is price and mix in a market whose units fell 16.7%. Regulation is the largest single threat to the services multiple: the Google default-search payment of about $20bn in 2022 is 18.3% of FY2025 services revenue and about 15% of operating income, the D.C. Circuit cross-appeal seeks a ban with a decision likely in 2027, and the EU fee schedule in force since 2026-10-01 charges 5% on externally distributed apps against 26% in-app. Catalysts score 4: the next twelve months are event-dense and mostly adversarial — results on 2026-11-02, Supreme Court review of link-out fees after certiorari on 2026-06-30, and the appeal in 2027 [S70, S76, S78].

The recommendation changes at identifiable points. A 46% gross margin, rather than the 47-48% base, takes FY2027 EPS to about $9.3 and fair value to $270 at 29 times, so the first entry tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount. A ban on the search payment removes 12.9% of EPS and, with a services de-rating, 15-20% of value, which moves the bear from $241 toward the $133 DCF. Services growth below 10% for two quarters removes about a tenth of the sum-of-the-parts value. On the other side, a December-quarter guide at or above 49% with FY2027 memory contracted would justify raising the base multiple from 29 to 31 times, about $303, still below the current price [S17, S99, S76].

Position sizing is zero today and staged thereafter. At $344.63 the probability-weighted return across the three scenarios is -15.4%, so the Kelly fraction is negative and the position is zero. At $270 the same weights give +7.8% against an -11% bear, an odds ratio of 0.70 that implies a full Kelly of about 39% of the fund — a number no single-stock process accepts, so a one-tenth fraction, 3.9%, sets the size and the 5% cap binds. The market regime reinforces patience: the VIX at 19.42 sits in the 77th percentile, the ten-year yields 4.93%, and technology has fallen 8.3% in a month against 0.9% for the SPY, the profile the regime playbook answers by discounting the target multiple 10-20% and scaling in with limit orders [S9, S10, S12, S25]. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and December-quarter guide on 2026-11-02.

Technology is the laggard, down 8.3% over one month against 0.9% for the SPY — a regime that penalises long-duration multiples [S7, S97, S8, S9, S10].

The business is not the problem. Apple converts profit into cash at 0.95-0.97 times net income on capex of 2.2% of revenue, holds $62,173M of net cash, and earns 40.3% of gross profit from services on 25.8% of revenue; a 30% revenue fall still leaves the company solvent and stops the buyback rather than breaking the balance sheet. What has changed is the margin: the June quarter's 50.1% gross margin carried two points of tariff refunds, memory costs have turned, and the base case underwrites 47-48% [S6, S17].

The price is the problem. At 39.5 times trailing and 35.2 times forward earnings against 18.09 times for the S&P 500, the shares discount a 7.0% cost of equity or 6.4-6.9% perpetual growth; the DCF at 9.0% is $212, the bull case $277, the sum of the parts $177-238, and the base scenario is $284, 18% below the close. The market is capitalising a peak margin and a peak multiple at the same time [S7, S97, S146].

Two facts would change the call. A gross margin at the low end of the range takes fair value to the first entry tranche, so the tranche becomes the base case rather than a discount to it; an appellate ban on the search payment moves the bear toward the discounted-cash-flow floor. The one question below decides which of the two the next twelve months delivers.

The view is non-consensus on price, not on franchise. The sell side's median target sits at the spot price, so the Street sees fair value where this analysis sees an overvaluation; the difference is the normalised margin and the exit multiple, not the quality of the installed base.

Positioning follows from that: zero today, a staged entry below the base case, and a sell discipline tied to the multiple and to services growth. The first hard test is the FY2026 10-K and the December-quarter guide on 2 November 2026, two days after this version.
